detail.abstract:
This article asks whether a state can remain a superpower while repeatedly failing in functions central to political success, and how such failures affect its credibility when seeking to reform political orders abroad. It rejects the classification of the United States as a conventionally failed state and develops two narrower concepts: selective functional failure and the external reform credibility paradox. Selective functional failure describes a durable gap between exceptional material capacity and weak, unequal, or reversible outcomes. The external reform credibility paradox explains how domestic fragility travels abroad through demonstration, diagnostic, commitment, accountability, and distributional deficits.

Using structured-focused comparison and a capacity–outcome framework, the study examines American war outcomes, democratic resilience, elite accountability, public health, firearms, incarceration, disaster recovery, alliance credibility, sanctions, and institutional withdrawal between 1975 and 2025, with evidence updated through 13 June 2026. The findings show that the United States can mobilize resources rapidly for military operations, financial rescue, and technological competition, yet frequently underperforms in producing durable peace, equal protection, universal human security, and predictable alliance leadership. The argument is neither isolationist nor a claim of moral equivalence. It advances a principle of reciprocity: a state that promotes rule of law, institutional reform, and democratic resilience abroad must subject itself to comparable standards of accountability and measurable outcomes at home.

title: Toward an Inclusive Textile Innovation Framework: Accessibility, Safety, and Sustainability at the Intersection of Fashion and Advanced Technology

detail.title: Toward an Inclusive Textile Innovation Framework: Accessibility, Safety, and Sustainability at the Intersection of Fashion and Advanced Technology

detail.abstract: The global fashion industry, valued at approximately USD 1.7 trillion annually, has historically failed to address the needs of three critical populations: the 2.2 billion individuals worldwide living with visual impairment or blindness (World Health Organization, 2023), newborns and young children vulnerable to abduction in the absence of protective technology, and all consumers affected by the ecological consequences of an industry responsible for approximately 10% of global carbon emissions (United Nations Environment Programme, 2019). This working paper introduces the Madison Color Innovation Model, a conceptual and applied framework developed by Mason Ewing, a blind Franco-Cameroonian-American entrepreneur and inventor based in Hollywood, California. The model proposes three interconnected innovations, each subject to patent applications filed with the United States Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO): (1) Braille Integrated into Textile (BIT), a system for the permanent tactile integration of functional Braille writing into fabric structure; (2) Luminous Braille Technology (LBT), a bimodal communication system combining tactile Braille encoding with luminous signaling integrated into smart textile fibers; and (3) Baby Lives Security (BLS), a dormant safety system embedded in organic newborn garments, activatable exclusively by law enforcement authorities in child abduction emergencies. These innovations are situated within the rapidly expanding smart textile market, projected to grow from USD 5.78 billion in 2024 to USD 20.76 billion by 2029 (Research and Markets, 2025), and are distinguished by their simultaneous integration of universal accessibility, embedded safety, and full eco-responsibility using certified organic materials. To the best of the author's knowledge, no prior commercially deployed or academically documented product integrates all three dimensions within a single fashion brand framework. This paper presents the theoretical foundations, market context, innovation descriptions, and implications for the field of inclusive textile design.

title: The Longs and Shorts of Hedge Funds
affiliations: The University of Hong Kong, National Taiwan University - Department of Finance and University of Rochester - Simon Business School

detail.title: The Longs and Shorts of Hedge Funds
detail.abstract: Using a novel dataset covering about one-fifth of the global hedge fund gross market value, we provide direct evidence on how hedge funds build and manage their portfolios. The dataset contains long vs. short positions and physical vs. synthetic positions at the daily level. Short (synthetic) positions account for roughly 45% (14%) of hedge funds' gross positions. Their net positions significantly predict future stock returns-the equal-weighted (value-weighted) high-low weekly quintile spread is 0.13% (0.17%). Quant funds' positions load heavily on academic factors, while equity longshort funds show weak alignment. Equity long-short funds' positions strongly forecast firms' earnings surprises and earn stronger earnings-day returns.

title: Private Assets in Defined Contribution Plans: A Comment Letter on the 2026 DOL Proposal
affiliations: and Duke University School of Law

detail.title: Private Assets in Defined Contribution Plans: A Comment Letter on the 2026 DOL Proposal
detail.abstract: This letter is written in response to the request by the Dept. of Labor for comments on “Fiduciary Duties in Selecting Designated Investment Alternatives,” published in 29 CFR Part 2550, RIN 1210-AC38. In this letter, we take issue with the basic premise underlying the DOL’s proposal to create a safe harbor that would facilitate large-scale retail investment in private markets through 401(k)s. Far from blessing the working public with valuable benefits from which they have unfairly been deprived, we argue that retail investment in private markets through 401(k) plans will give retail investors little upside in exchange for taking on substantial new risks and heavy fees, all while eroding the features that have historically made private markets special. We also argue that 401(k) plan fiduciaries are poorly equipped to serve the best interests of 401(k) plan beneficiaries in private market investments, and we respectfully urge the department to reconsider the regulation.

title: The Structural Liquidity Factor: Persistent Alpha Beyond Fama-French

detail.title: The Structural Liquidity Factor: Persistent Alpha Beyond Fama-French
detail.abstract: Standard asset pricing theory predicts that no zero-beta strategy should earn above the risk-free rate. We document a systematic violation of this prediction that has persisted for seventeen years across four macroeconomic crises and six independent robustness batteries. The BLT Engine — a systematic trading strategy derived from structural FX microstructure — generates +3.98%/year of annualized alpha (t = +4.37, p < 0.0001) with near-zero market beta (βm = +0.021, R² = 0.005) across 664 trades from 2008 to 2025, validated on Bloomberg BQuant institutional infrastructure. This alpha survives the complete Fama-French five-factor model and Carhart momentum, is orthogonal to all known FX risk premia (carry, momentum, value, dollar factor), and leaves 97.38% of return variance structurally unexplained after eleven factors. Crisis performance reinforces rather than weakens this evidence: the strategy generated +18.2% while the S&P 500 lost −33.1% during the Lehman collapse, with geometric invariance confirmed across calm and crisis regimes (t = 0.080, p = 0.936). Walk-forward analysis confirms an OOS/IS Sharpe ratio of 0.76× across four unseen periods, ruling out structural overfitting. We interpret these findings as evidence for a missing Structural Liquidity Factor (FSL) arising from post-2008 FX microstructure — a persistent, capacity-constrained premium that standard asset pricing models were not designed to capture and have systematically failed to price since at least 2008.

detail.abstract: The United States is facing a well-documented national shortage of qualified educators-and federal data confirms that this issue extends far beyond simple hiring gaps. According to the National Center for Education Statistics (NCES), U.S. Department of Education, approximately 74% of public schools reported difficulty filling teaching positions with fully qualified candidates for the 2024-2025 school year. At the same time, only about 79% of teaching vacancies were filled with fully certified teachers, meaning a significant share of classrooms are staffed by individuals who are not fully qualified for their roles. This is not a temporary disruption. It is a structural workforce challenge.

title: The Boutgajouft Invariance Score (bis): A Distribution-Free Test for Structural Alpha in Systematic Trading Strategies

detail.title: The Boutgajouft Invariance Score (bis): A Distribution-Free Test for Structural Alpha in Systematic Trading Strategies
detail.abstract: We introduce the Boutgajouft Invariance Score (BIS), a novel distribution-free metric that tests whether a systematic trading strategy generates structural alpha — alpha arising from a persistent geometric attractor — as opposed to a regime-contingent or statistically spurious premium. The BIS requires only the output distribution of trade-level R-multiples and is entirely agnostic to the signal-generating mechanism, enabling academic validation without intellectual property disclosure. The metric formalizes three invariance properties predicted by structural factor theory: (P1) cross-sectional invariance across subsamples, (P2) invariance across volatility regimes, and (P3) temporal invariance across holding periods. We derive the BIS as a normalized composite of Wasserstein-1 distances across these three dimensions and establish its null distribution via stationary block bootstrap (B = 10,000). Applied to 21 systematic strategies spanning FX, equity, cross-asset, and volatility strategy classes (2008-2025), the BIS correctly discriminates structural from regime-dependent strategies with near-perfect discriminant validity: Spearman ρ = 0.9996 (p < 0.0001, n = 21). The BLT Engine (BIS = 0.0658, 95% CI [0.0435, 0.1835]), a proprietary FX structural strategy, is the sole structural classifier in the sample; all 20 benchmark strategies fall in the semi-structural or regime-dependent range (BIS ∈ [0.18, 0.38]). Mann-Whitney tests confirm that the BLT Engine BIS is significantly lower than all benchmarks (p < 0.001). Power tests demonstrate near-perfect detection of structural breaks (power ≥ 0.997 across all scenarios). The BIS provides the first quantitative framework for distinguishing structural from statistical alpha without requiring signal disclosure, with direct applications to institutional due diligence, academic factor validation, and regulatory review.

detail.abstract: This article synthesizes review-level scholarship on renewable energy certificates (RECs) and adjacent energy-attribute instruments as a preliminary stage of a broader systematic literature review (SLR) focused on I-RECs and related certificate markets. The corpus was drawn from review records identified during the screening workflow of a wider REC-centered SLR protocol, aligned with PRISMA 2020 guidelines. Following deduplication and relevance screening, twelve substantive reviews were retained for synthesis. These reviews were classified into three analytical groups: comprehensive reviews, single-topic reviews, and tracking-technology reviews. The article addresses six research questions: (RQ1) the mechanisms employed to develop RECs; (RQ2) whether RECs contribute to investment in renewable generation and storage; (RQ3) how regulatory frameworks and policy designs shape certificate effectiveness; (RQ4) which technologies are used to prevent double counting; (RQ5) which business models and market actors generate RECs; and (RQ6) what principal gaps remain in the review literature. The findings reveal that the review field is heterogeneous and remains conceptually fragmented. A recurring pattern is that certificate systems do not function in isolation; rather, they are typically embedded in broader policy mixes that include renewable portfolio standards, feed-in tariffs, carbon markets, green power trading, disclosure systems, and corporate accounting standards. Evidence on investment effects is suggestive but uneven and tends to be strongest when certificates are tied to scarcity, clear retirement rules, credible registries, and demand from compliance obligations or premium voluntary buyers. The literature further indicates that double-counting prevention depends less on the certificate label itself than on governance architecture-encompassing registry design, issuance controls, retirement procedures, residual-mix treatment, and, increasingly, digital traceability infrastructure. Brazil is represented in the review literature as a rapidly maturing voluntary market, particularly through the articulation between I-REC/I-TRACK architecture, REC Brazil sustainability attributes, and more recent institutional innovations such as the CCEE certification platform. Significant gaps nonetheless persist, most notably with respect to causal evidence on additionality, storage incentives, and crosscountry comparability. The article concludes that this review clarifies the conceptual terrain, refines the coding logic for the forthcoming SLR, and identifies a more rigorous agenda for future research.

title: Can Borrower-based Measures Shield Banks from Loan Losses?
affiliations: International Monetary Fund (IMF),  and International Monetary Fund (IMF)

detail.title: Can Borrower-based Measures Shield Banks from Loan Losses?
detail.abstract: This paper examines empirically whether borrower-based macroprudential measures can increase the resilience of banks. Using a newly built index of time-varying restrictiveness of borrower-based measures and bank-level data in 31 countries, our study sheds new light on interactions between macroeconomic pressures and macroprudential policies: Higher interest rates increase loan loss provisions for banks offering flexible-rate loans, but this effect is attenuated when borrower-based measures have been tight in years preceding high rates. Tighter macroprudential settings also contain the impact of unemployment on loan loss provisions, further strengthening banks’ resilience to shocks.

title: Democracy in the Air: Uncounted Emissions, Discounted Communities
affiliations: Cornell University - Law School

detail.title: Democracy in the Air: Uncounted Emissions, Discounted Communities
detail.abstract: Climate change is a collective action problem exacerbated by gaps in our democratic systems. These gaps include disrupted mechanisms for accountability, distorted systems of knowledge, and policies which exclude community participation. While many components of climate law produce these democratic failures, greenhouse gas accounting practices have, for the most part, received limited scrutiny for the ways they undermine progress on climate change. Many subnational governments have committed to reducing greenhouse gas emissions as part of their climate policies. In so doing, they produce greenhouse gas inventories-accounts of jurisdictional emissions-against which they can assess the success of mitigation measures. Yet these greenhouse gas inventories may be incomplete, leading to "unaccounted-for", or excluded, emissions. This Article illustrates the impacts that poor, incomplete, and inaccurate greenhouse gas accounting has in exacerbating environmental injustices. It focuses on Stockton, California, where it highlights how emissions from industries such as aviation, maritime shipping, and stationary sources are excluded from the City of Stockton's greenhouse gas inventory. Finally, it illustrates opportunities to account for these emissions as an additional tool for environmental justice and democratic governance.

title: My Law and Language Experience of the U.S. and Indonesia

detail.title: My Law and Language Experience of the U.S. and Indonesia
detail.abstract: In the U.S., constitutional law constantly evolves, and the doctrine—particularly of the First Amendment—is far from straightforward. Like corporate law, the country’s constitutional law is one of the most innovative legal fields in the world. On the crux of the complexity of legal interpretation, legal language, it takes more than a language to understand the law. To understand the law of a country, however, requires one to first ‘speak’ the language. So, what does the law mean in a language? This field is far from settled and Constitutional interpretation, no matter which country, cannot be to be settled, and in need of more intensive academic enquiry. What a Supreme Court wrote in 1950, for example, may have vastly different meaning 100 years later. It takes more than a language to understand the law.

title: Procurement Design with Network Effects: A Case Study in Infrastructure
affiliations: Columbia University - Columbia Business School, Decision Risk and Operations, Yale School of Management and Stanford Graduate School of Business

detail.title: Procurement Design with Network Effects: A Case Study in Infrastructure
detail.abstract: Problem definition. Expanding infrastructure in transport, energy, and digital sectors is important for achieving the economic and sustainability goals of many developing economies. The values of projects involving such infrastructure expansion can be interdependent due to inherent network effects. However, institutional constraints and limited coordination capacity often force governments to award projects through separate auctions. Brazil’s National Logistics Plan (PNL) exemplifies this setting, where interdependent transport investments are procured separately despite strong network effects across projects. We study how a government buyer should design separate per-project procurements when the overall value depends on the resulting infrastructure network, and bundling is not feasible. Methodology/results. We analyze: (i) parallel procurement, in which auction rules are fixed in advance; (ii) sequential procurement, in which their sequence is fixed, but later rules can adapt to earlier executed projects. In both settings, we show that the optimal mechanism retains a simple form akin to canonical results in auction theory: each project is awarded to the lowest virtual-cost bidder if its virtual cost falls below a project-specific threshold that reflects its expected contribution to the equilibrium-induced network. Beyond the optimal mechanism, we propose a simple and interpretable ``credit-aware'' heuristic that adjusts each project's threshold by a simple one-step estimate of its expected network contribution. To demonstrate the importance of network effects in procurement design, we construct a calibrated case study of a major railroad corridor expansion under the PNL. Modeling the Brazilian infrastructure as a hub--spoke network, and the expansion as two key added segments, we estimate their network effect by solving a congestion game aligned with current practice. We show that joint commissioning of these segments adds 16.4% additional economic value, and the common practice of ignoring network effect in procurement design leaves 30–36% of attainable surplus unrealized. Our credit-aware heuristic recovers about 90% of the optimal surplus. Managerial implications. As developing economies invest in infrastructure expansion, it is important to evaluate these projects holistically, as network effects can be strong and first-order. Even when institutional constraints require projects to be procured separately, network effects can still be incorporated effectively through careful adjustments to existing mechanisms, and even simple changes can yield substantial economic and environmental gains.

title: Age-Dependent Brain Mechanics Are Linked to Microstructural Changes
affiliations: Technology University of Braunschweig, RWTH Aachen University, University of Veterinary Medicine Hannover - Veterinary-Endocrinology and laboratory diagnostics, Stanford University and Technology University of Braunschweig

detail.title: Age-Dependent Brain Mechanics Are Linked to Microstructural Changes
detail.abstract: Accurate knowledge of brain tissue mechanics is essential for understanding mechanically induced pathologies and developing reliable computational models of brain injury and neurosurgical interventions. However, the age-related changes in brain mechanics and their microstructural basis are not fully understood. In this study, we examined age-related changes in brain mechanics and microstructure in porcine tissue across five age groups, from early development to young adulthood. Mechanical tests in tension and compression were performed in different anatomical regions, including an anisotropic characterization of the corpus callosum. We used Bayesian parameter identification to estimate material parameters based on isotropic Ogden and anisotropic Gasser-Ogden-Holzapfel models. Meanwhile, histological analyses quantified myelin, cell, glia, and neuron measures. Our results revealed nonlinear age dependencies of tensile and compressive mechanics accompanied by clear age-dependent microstructural differences. Notably, myelin- and glia-related measures were the most consistent positive correlates of stiffness. Mediation analysis further suggested that microstructure, particularly glia-related features, serves as a measurable intermediate link between age and mechanics. These findings provide a microstructurally informed basis for more realistic, age-dependent, computational brain models.

title: Gamification, Motivation, and Contradiction: A Critical Analysis of Duolingo

detail.title: Gamification, Motivation, and Contradiction: A Critical Analysis of Duolingo
detail.abstract: Gamification, defined as the use of game-like elements in non-game contexts, has become a prevalent strategy in digital learning environments. Platforms such as Duolingo have successfully integrated badges, streaks, leaderboards, and daily XP systems into their interfaces, aiming to enhance user engagement and retention. The popularity and commercial success of these platforms have led many developers to replicate similar motivational systems all across the education sector. Gamified systems, while being effective at improving user engagement, sometimes employ dark patterns: designs that covertly manipulate user behaviour in ways that benefit the developers, often at the expense of user autonomy or well-being. The term “dark pattern” originates in user experience (UX) research and refers to interface strategies that trick users into decisions they might not otherwise make. When applied in learning contexts, such patterns may distort users' relationship with the initial learning objectives by pressuring them to interact not out of curiosity or internal motivation, but to avoid negative feedback or penalties. This essay takes the popular language learning app Duolingo, and examines it under the lense of Self-Determination Theory and Dark patterns.

title: Stagflation Trap for Japan: A Two-Sector Endogenous Growth Model with Directed Search

detail.title: Stagflation Trap for Japan: A Two-Sector Endogenous Growth Model with Directed Search
detail.abstract: We extend the stagnation trap framework of Benigno and Fornaro (2018) to a two-sector economy with directed search labor markets, employment protection, and capital-embodied technical change. Our model generates three distinct equilibria—a growth equilibrium, a deflationary stagnation trap, and a supply-side stagflation equilibrium—each with characteristic inflation, employment, and wage dynamics. The key mechanism operates through sectoral labor reallocation: when pessimistic growth expectations make R&D unprofitable, automationdriven displacement in the capital-intensive sector halts, triggering labor hoarding. The resulting scarcity in the labor-intensive sector generates Baumol cost disease, producing stagflation even absent demand-pull pressures. We calibrate the model to Japan’s experience, where declining population, rising college attainment, and rigid employment protection produce the conditions for all three equilibria. Escaping the deflationary stagnation trap does not necessarily restore the growth equilibrium: if sectoral labor misallocation is left unaddressed, supply-side deterioration leads the economy into a stagflation trap with positive inflation but persistently low growth.

title: Macro Policies Through a HANK Model Lens: Monetary, Fiscal, Government Debt, and the Maturity Structure of Debt 1

detail.title: Macro Policies Through a HANK Model Lens: Monetary, Fiscal, Government Debt, and the Maturity Structure of Debt 1
detail.abstract: This paper provides a rigorous welfare analysis of monetary, fiscal, and government debt maturity policies within a non-linear Heterogeneous-Agent New Keynesian (HANK) framework. We depart from the standard assumption of fixed portfolios by endogenizing household optimization across multiple asset classes over the wealth distribution. By integrating Preferred-Habitat theory into the HANK structure, we endogenize the term premium and identify a novel 'Duration-Sensitive Wealth Effect'. To capture the complex non-linear transition dynamics that conventional log-linear approximations overlook, we employ the Sequence-Space Jacobian (SSJ) method alongside the Extended Method of Endogenous Gridpoints (EGM). The model is disciplined by Korean micro-data (SHFW), which reflects a unique environment of high real-asset concentration (75.5%) and rapidly evolving debt maturity profiles. Our findings demonstrate that debt maturity management—specifically Operation Twist—functions as a potent, independent redistribution mechanism that operates even when the aggregate debt level remains unchanged. By shifting the term premium and revaluing long-duration assets, these policies generate heterogeneous welfare effects driven by differences in household duration exposure and marginal propensities to consume (MPCs). Our results highlight that debt maturity structure is not merely a financing tool but a fundamental determinant of macroeconomic stabilization and distributional outcomes

detail.abstract: This paper develops a unified normative and political-economy framework for evaluating artificial intelligence (AI) as a structural force reshaping human welfare, dignity, and moral agency. Part III serves two interconnected functions. First, it establishes the constraint geometry that governs the dynamic optimization problems of Part IV: drawing on the convergence of major civilizational moral traditions — Catholic social teaching, Kantian deontology, the capability approach, Confucian ethics, and Islamic ethics — it formalizes dignity and agency as lexicographically prior, non-contractible constraints on admissible AI trajectories, and defines the set of forbidden technolog ical regimes F whose operation necessarily violates these constraints. Second, it operationalizes the multi-dimensional welfare function W(Y,S,D,C,L) as an estimable political-economy framework, decomposing AI’s effects into four channels — productivity augmentation (p), labor displacement (q), surveillance (r), and autonomy erosion (s) — and establishing a formal bridge between production-side parameters and welfare-side dimensions. The central theoretical contribution is the Welfare Decoupling Theorem: there exist economically plausible AI trajectories along which output rises while comprehensive welfare falls, driven by negative contributions through the dignity, agency, and community channels. The paper further demonstrates that welfare inequality can increase without any corresponding rise in income inequality, and characterizes the conditions under which dignity-constrained AI governance weakly dominates market-regulated and unregulated regimes. An empirical strategy — combining instrumental variables, difference-in-differences, and shift-share identification, each with explicit validity conditions — is proposed for taking the framework to data.

detail.abstract: Why do firms with broadly similar resource positions and operating in broadly similar competitive contexts produce divergent sustained competitive advantage outcomes? Resource orchestration theory specifies the synchronisation of structuring, bundling, and leveraging processes through which managerial action converts resources into advantage (Sirmon et al., 2007), but has not theorised how orchestration capacity is allocated across competing strategic horizons under bounded capacity, how orchestration actions compound through temporally extended trajectories, how the three regimes of outpacing, parity, and lagging produce distinct dynamic effects on the productive zone, or how strategic-group-level competitive intensity itself emerges from the distribution of orchestration paths across rival firms. This paper develops a Path-Based Theory of Resource Orchestration, operationalised through the Dual-Horizon Resource Orchestration under Constraint framework. The theory introduces five analytic constructs: dual-horizon orchestration intent as a meta-orchestration layer directing capacity across competing short-horizon and longhorizon orientations; the productive zone as a band bounded by a maintenance threshold below and a monetisation ceiling above; the orchestration path as the temporally extended trajectory through which firms produce or fail to produce sustained advantage; the strategic group as the level at which competitive intensity is theorised (Caves and Porter, 1977; Porter, 1980); and capability stocks and capability deltas as the distinct level and rate variables that connect firmlevel orchestration to arena-level dynamics (Dierickx and Cool, 1989). Seven propositions specify the operating mechanisms: asymmetric crowding-out at the strategic layer, sequence-determined compounding at the operational layer, the productive-zone constraint, a lexicographic priority allocation rule as the efficient frontier of orchestration with six identifiable failure modes, an intent-bounded feedback mechanism, regime-specific dynamics through which the productive zone widens for outpacing firms, holds in lockstep for parity firms, and narrows self-reinforcingly for lagging firms, and a strategic-group-level co-evolutionary mechanism through which the rate of change in competitive intensity is jointly produced by the skewness and stock-weighted distribution of capability deltas across rival firms. The theory integrates resource orchestration with Penrosian growth theory, behavioural-strategy traditions, and the strategic-groups tradition, offering a multi-level process-theoretic account of capability-driven growth-failure dynamics under universally bounded orchestration capacity across the for-profit competitive sector.

title: Astrology, Political Leadership, and the Economic Performance of Nations, 19602026: An Interdisciplinary Political Economy Investigation

detail.title: Astrology, Political Leadership, and the Economic Performance of Nations, 19602026: An Interdisciplinary Political Economy Investigation

detail.abstract: This paper develops a large-scale interdisciplinary research programme investigating whether the astrological and horoscopic characteristics of national political leaders are systematically associated with long-run economic growth and human development outcomes across countries during the 19602026 period. Four classes of political-leadership variables are constructed: (i) an astrological index based on elemental and modal celestial classications; (ii) a zodiac index capturing the distribution of leaders across the twelve solar signs; (iii) a horoscopic index incorporating natal-chart features where birth-time data permit; and (iv) a composite cosmology leadership index (CCLI) aggregating the three sub-indices. These measures are merged with international macroeconomic and human development datasets and estimated within an augmented Amavilah growth-model framework that encompasses Solow-Swan, endogenous-growth, and institutional-quality determinants. The analysis is motivated not by metaphysical commitment to astrology, but by broader questions regarding symbolic systems, political psychology, elite recruitment, institutional behaviour, collective belief structures, and nonlinear determinants of economic performance. Five formal hypotheses are stated and subjected to panel econometric tests using xed-e ects, dynamic GMM, quantile, and threshold regression estimators, together with a comprehensive battery of robustness checks addressing multiple testing, selection endogeneity, and omitted-variable bias. The paper argues that even if astrology itself lacks physical causal validity, astrological belief systems may shape political behaviour, social expectations, leadership selection, symbolic legitimacy, and institutional decision-making in ways potentially observable in macro-development data. The epistemological contribution of the paper is therefore as much about clarifying the limits of symbolic explanation in economics as about establishing positive empirical findings.

detail.abstract: War economies, sanctions regimes, hyperinflation, blockade risk, and digital disruption compress the time horizons on which conventional corporate strategy depends. In such environments, the problem is not only that risk increases; it is that decision makers confront Knightian uncertainty, capital immobility, unstable feedback, and ethical exposure. This article develops Purposeful Plurality as a firm-level strategy model for such conditions. Purposeful Plurality is defined as the deliberate translation of a coherent macro-vision into a governed portfolio of modular, sub-annual, reversible micro-projects. The model contributes to three scholarly conversations: strategy under uncertainty and real options, dynamic capabilities and strategic agility, and firms in conflict-affected markets. It argues that firms in extreme contexts should not abandon strategic direction; rather, they should pluralize execution while centralizing intent through a strategic spine, liquidity discipline, boundary rules, and high-frequency learning. The article distinguishes Purposeful Plurality from financial real options, effectuation, bricolage, resilience, ambidexterity, and lean experimentation. It also repairs common citation risks by treating Iran’s 2026 war economy, Dubai-style geographic hedging, and Tehran’s municipal micro-project logic as illustrative extreme-stress contexts, not as settled empirical proof. The result is a theory of operational optionality: how organizations create real-option-like flexibility through micro-project architecture when formal option valuation, long-horizon forecasting, and large irreversible commitments become unreliable.

title: Humanity, Dignity, and Artificial Intelligence Part I: Papal Insights on Human Flourishing in the Age of Algorithmic Systems: A Formal Welfare-Theoretic Analysis

detail.title: Humanity, Dignity, and Artificial Intelligence Part I: Papal Insights on Human Flourishing in the Age of Algorithmic Systems: A Formal Welfare-Theoretic Analysis

contentType.other: Working Paper Part I of IV in a project called Humanity, Dignity, and Artificial Intelligence

detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence has revived fundamental questions concerning human dignity, moral agency, economic organization, and the future of human flourishing. This paper examines these questions through a dual lens: insights drawn from the papal social tradition—particularly Pope Francis and Pope Leo XIV—and the formal tools of welfare economics, social choice theory, and the economics of information. We argue that contemporary debates about artificial intelligence ultimately depend upon deeper assumptions regarding the human person, social welfare, and the common good that standard neoclassical frameworks leave implicit or elide altogether. Pope Francis challenges the moral incompleteness of conventional welfare economics by emphasizing solidarity, fraternity, ecological stewardship, and the irreducibility of human dignity to preference satisfaction. Pope Leo XIV extends this critique into the age of artificial intelligence by questioning the subordination of the human person to algorithmic systems, the concentration of computational power, and the erosion of epistemic autonomy. Together, these papal interventions constitute a coherent critique of what we term technocratic welfarism: the tendency to evaluate social arrangements solely by aggregate output, efficiency, or revealed preference, while bracketing the structural conditions under which preferences are formed and human agency is exercised. The paper develops a formal human-centered welfare framework, denoted W, that extends the standard Bergson–Samuelson social welfare function to include dignity, social cohesion, moral agency, ecological sustainability, and relational goods. A key result is a decomposition theorem showing that the welfare derivative with respect to artificial intelligence is generally ambiguous in sign: AI may increase material output while simultaneously reducing welfare when it erodes dignity, community cohesion, or authentic moral agency. We further introduce a dignity constraint analogous to a Rawlsian lexicographic priority rule, and show conditions under which unconstrained AI optimization violates this constraint. Applications are developed in the areas of labor market displacement, algorithmic governance, epistemic autonomy, and the distribution of AI-generated surplus. The paper also engages the economics of artificial general intelligence concentration, analyzing how winner-take-all dynamics in AI development create rent extraction, dependency, and asymmetric power relations that papal social thought identifies as incompatible with human dignity and subsidiarity. We conclude by sketching the architecture of a dignity-preserving AI governance regime and its relationship to the common good tradition.

title: Performance-Based Attrition and Decreasing Returns to Scale
affiliations: University of Queensland and David Eccles School of Business, University of Utah

detail.title: Performance-Based Attrition and Decreasing Returns to Scale
detail.abstract: In interpreting fund flows and performance in active management, the explanatory power of the Berk and Green (2004) framework depends on the magnitude of decreasing returns to scale (DRS)-the degree to which fund size erodes performance. Existing DRS estimators, most notably the recursive demeaning of Zhu (2018), produce puzzlingly large estimates. We show that such estimates overstate DRS due to performance-based attrition: funds are more likely to close after poor performance. We develop a new estimator that isolates within-fund DRS effects by controlling for between-fund skill-size matching while remaining robust to performance-based attrition. When applied to U.S. active equity mutual funds, our estimator delivers DRS estimates that are statistically significant but economically plausible, roughly an order of magnitude lower than some previous estimates.

title: The Strategic Impact of Cheaper Ad Production
affiliations: University of Maryland - Robert H. Smith School of Business and University of Maryland, Smith School of Business

detail.title: The Strategic Impact of Cheaper Ad Production
detail.abstract: Generative AI is reducing the cost of producing advertising creatives by enabling firms to generate, personalize, and test many ad variants at scale. We study how such reductions in ad-production cost affect advertising strategy, ad pricing, and the allocation of efficiency gains between advertisers and an upstream ad seller. We develop a game-theoretic model of duopoly competition in which advertising creates awareness only when consumers are both exposed to an ad and pay attention to it. Firms can increase effective reach through two margins: breadth, by purchasing more impressions, or depth, by producing higher-quality creatives that increase attention conditional on exposure. Lower production costs induce firms to substitute from broad distribution of generic ads toward narrower distribution of higher-quality ads. This breadth-depth substitution generates a non-monotonic relationship between production cost and the ad seller's optimal price: as production cost falls, ad prices first decrease because demand for impressions declines, but later increase because higher creative quality raises advertisers' willingness to pay for exposure. Consequently, improvements in creative-production technology can reduce total advertising output and effective reach. Moreover, lower production costs can reduce advertisers' profits by shifting surplus toward the ad seller. These results identify a novel mechanism through which efficiency gains are appropriated in advertising markets.

title: When Institutions Cannot Keep Up with Artificial Intelligence: Expiration Theory and the Risk of Institutional Invalidation

detail.title: When Institutions Cannot Keep Up with Artificial Intelligence: Expiration Theory and the Risk of Institutional Invalidation
detail.abstract: As Artificial Intelligence systems increasingly surpass or replace traditional human roles, institutions founded on beliefs in human cognitive superiority, moral authority, and procedural oversight encounter a more profound challenge than mere disruption: expiration. This paper posits that, instead of being outperformed, many legacy institutions are becoming epistemically misaligned with the realities of AIdriven environments. To clarify this change, the paper presents the Expiration Theory. This conceptual model interprets institutional collapse not as a market failure but as the erosion of fundamental assumptions amid technological shifts. In addition, the paper introduces the AI Pressure Clock, a diagnostic tool that categorises institutions based on their vulnerability to AI disruption and their capacity to adapt to it. Through an analysis across sectors including law, healthcare, education, finance, and creative industries, the paper illustrates how certain systems are nearing functional obsolescence, while others are actively restructuring their foundational norms. As a conceptual study, the paper concludes by highlighting the theoretical, policy, and leadership ramifications, asserting that institutional survival in the age of AI relies not solely on digital capabilities but also on the capacity to redefine the core principles of legitimacy, authority, and decision-making.

title: The Allen Operating System: Trust-Bearing Distribution and the Hidden Business Architecture of Byron Allen’s Media Company.

detail.abstract:
This paper develops the Allen Operating System as an analytical framework for understanding the business architecture of Byron Allen's media company. Rather than treating Allen Media Group as a conventional entertainment company built around prestige programming, celebrity, or critical approval, the paper argues that Allen's business logic centers on undervalued distribution, owned or controlled supply, direct monetization, cost discipline, and compounding across multiple media surfaces. The analysis traces this operating system from Allen's early transition from performer to owner through syndication, court shows, CBS late night, The Weather Channel, Local Now, BuzzFeed, HuffPost, Tasty, and his stated ambition to compete with YouTube in free, ad-supported video. 

The paper's central contribution is the concept of trust-bearing distribution. Allen's acquisitions and time-buy arrangements are not simply cheap or distressed media plays; they often involve assets that retain usable trust, habit, utility, audience memory, advertiser comfort, local relevance, or brand recognition. The Weather Channel is examined as a key case: after IBM acquired The Weather Company's digital and product businesses, Allen acquired the television network, which still carried the consumer-facing trust surface of weather as a daily-use and emergency-information category. The CBS late-night deal and the court-show portfolio further illustrate the distinction between performer, supplier, and operator: Allen places repeatable owned supply inside distribution surfaces and seeks to control the commercial inventory around them. 

The framework developed here presents Allen's model as a repeatable business logic rather than a formal doctrine. Its power lies in identifying trust-bearing surfaces that others misclassify, placing controlled supply inside those surfaces, monetizing the relationship directly, and connecting enough surfaces that the operator's influence becomes harder to ignore. The result is a business strategy that is less about prestige and more about access, inventory, trust, and operating control.

title: Capstone Capitalism and the Portfolio Turn:  Credential Rent Extraction, Immaterial Labour, and the Policical Economy of Production-Based Formation

detail.title: Capstone Capitalism and the Portfolio Turn:  Credential Rent Extraction, Immaterial Labour, and the Policical Economy of Production-Based Formation
detail.abstract: This paper develops a political economy critique of the contemporary credential system in higher education, theorising it as capstone capitalism: a structural tendency of late-capitalist educational institutions to concentrate institutional investment in the credential-the exchange-value capstone of the formation process-while systematically underinvesting in the substantive formation processes through which genuine cognitive, social, and affective capabilities are developed. We formally specify capstone capitalism's constitutive conditions and distinguish it from adjacent concepts in the rent-seeking and human capital literatures. Drawing on Autonomist Marxist analysis-specifically Negri and Hardt's (2000, 2009) theorisation of Empire and the general intellect, and Virno's (2004) analysis of the multitude-we develop the argument that the credential apparatus functions as a mechanism for the appropriation and commodification of cognitive capacities whose formation substantially exceeds the formal educational encounter. We locate this analysis within Bourdieu's field theory and demonstrate how credential rent extraction is sustained intergenerationally through the conversion of class-specific habitus into institutionally certified academic capital. Structural data from OECD and national educational systems on credential inflation, student debt growth, employer training investment, and graduate wage premiums provides empirical evidence for the rent-extraction thesis. We then examine whether studio-based, production-oriented formation models represent a redistributive alternative to credential rent extraction or a sophisticated extension of human capital externalisation. We argue that the distinction turns on four structural conditions, with particular attention to the habitus development mechanism through which studio formation specifically addresses the cultural capital differential, and to Standing's (2011) precariat analysis as the class-formation dimension of credential inflation. Counterarguments are engaged throughout.

title: Knowledge as Volume: A Geometric Approach to Human Capital Measurement

detail.title: Knowledge as Volume: A Geometric Approach to Human Capital Measurement

contentType.other: Working Paper -- Third Revised and Extended Version

detail.abstract: Human capital is conventionally measured using years of schooling, educational attainment, or related proxies. Such measures foreground the quantity dimension of knowledge while systematically neglecting quality and temporal dynamics. This paper develops a rigorous geometric framework in which knowledge is represented as a three-dimensional stock characterized by three orthogonal dimensions: quantity (Q), quality (q), and time (t). Modelled as a Cobb-Douglas volume function K(Q, q, t) = AQ α q β t γ , knowledge is interpreted as a volume rather than a scalar or planar area. We derive closed-form expressions for the cumulative knowledge stock via triple integration over a rectangular domain, characterise all first and second partial derivatives, establish the positive complementarity of all three dimensions through the sign of the cross-partial derivatives, and formalise a quantity-quality tradeoff that mirrors the grade-tonnage relationship in geological engineering. We embed the framework within endogenous growth theory, distinguishing it from Mincerian and Lucas-type specifications, introduce a dynamic generalisation with time-varying elasticities, and discuss aggregation from individual to economy-wide stocks. The paper concludes with a detailed agenda for empirical implementation, including identification strategies and a multidimensional Knowledge Volume Index for crosscountry analysis.

title: Workforce Readiness and Article 4 AI Literacy Compliance: Obligations, Programme Design, and Sector-Specific Implementation

detail.abstract: , is the most pervasive obligation in the regulatory framework. It requires providers and deployers to take measures to ensure, to their best extent, a sufficient level of AI literacy of their staff and other persons dealing with the operation and use of AI systems on their behalf. The obligation applies to all AI system contexts and amplifies the Article 26(2) competence requirement for high-risk AI operations. Research indicates a significant workforce readiness gap. McKinsey's 2025 Superagency in the Workplace report finds that 46% of organisations cite talent skill gaps as the leading barrier to AI adoption. The OECD Skills Outlook 2023 finds that fewer than 1% of online vacancies for AI professionals mentioned AI ethics or responsible AI in the majority of the 14 OECD countries surveyed. Health Education England's workforce confidence research finds that targeted training is needed across all clinical archetypes and that current educational provision is fragmentary. This paper analyses the legal architecture of Article 4 and its interaction with Article 26(2), proposes a five-tier audience segmentation model with content and assessment specifications for each tier, examines sectoral implementation in financial services, healthcare, and employment, integrates the literacy obligation with ISO/IEC 42001:2023 Section 7.2 competence management, and discusses the European Commission and OECD AILit framework as an external reference.

title: Public Administration in the Federated States of Micronesia

detail.title: Public Administration in the Federated States of Micronesia
detail.abstract: Public administration in the Federated States of Micronesia (FSM) operates within a complex environment shaped by history, culture, geography, and limited institutional capacity. As citizens increasingly expect improved services, stronger accountability, economic opportunities, and climate resilience, the pressure for administrative reform has intensified. This paper examines the development of public administration in the FSM since independence, identifies major obstacles that continue to hinder reform, and evaluates recent initiatives aimed at strengthening governance. Drawing on government documents, audit reports from the Office of the National Public Auditor, the Strategic Development Plan, and peerreviewed governance scholarship, this paper outlines practical strategies for longterm improvement. The analysis suggests that sustainable reform requires investment in human resources, stronger coordination between national and state governments, realistic approaches to digital modernization, and meaningful engagement with traditional leadership.

The research received no external funding and was not influenced by any third party. No other competing interests are declared.

detail.abstract:
Brands often run promotions tied to culturally salient events: a national team winning a tournament, a weather event, a major entertainment outcome. From a marketing perspective these are creative campaigns; from a finance perspective they are event-contingent liabilities whose cost depends on an external resolution. A prediction market quotes the price of payoff contingent on a specific event resolution. A brand can hedge the campaign's exposure at this price, converting an uncertain liability into a deterministic cost, and can read the same price back into the reward it advertises. This paper calls that mechanism PredictBack. Its central equation is:

                                                                𝑅 𝑖 = 𝑏/ 𝑘 ⋅ 𝑝 𝑖 

where 𝑅 𝑖 is the headline reward rate for outcome 𝑖, 𝑏 is the promotional budget rate per unit of transaction value, 𝑘 is the economic cost coefficient of the reward, and 𝑝 𝑖 is the prediction-market price of the contract that pays out under 𝐸 𝑖. Lower-priced outcomes support larger headline rewards at the same hedged cost. The result reframes conditional promotions as priced, hedgeable liabilities tied to public uncertainty, and prediction markets as pricing infrastructure for promotional budgets, beyond their use in forecasting.

title: Supply-Chain Disruptions: Penalty for Starting a Cascade, or Reward for Stopping One?
affiliations: Shanghai Jiao Tong University (SJTU) - Antai College of Economics and Management and NUS Business School - Department of Decision Sciences

detail.title: Supply-Chain Disruptions: Penalty for Starting a Cascade, or Reward for Stopping One?
detail.abstract: Problem definition: Supply-chain contracts often compensate downstream firms for the realized costs of absorbing upstream disruptions, such as expedited freight, alternative sourcing, overtime production, or line-restart expenses. However, these contracts rarely compensate firms for preventing disruption cascades and the downstream losses their recovery actions avert. We study how a platform or supply-chain control tower should design settlement rules that incentivize firms both to prevent disruptions from propagating and to absorb shocks that have already arrived. Methodology/results: We model a sequential supply chain as a two-state stochastic process in which each agent privately chooses prevention investment under normal operations and absorption investment after receiving disrupted inputs from upstream. We introduce the notion of a "continuation-value gap," which measures the marginal system harm from leaving the chain in a cascading state rather than restoring normal operations. This continuationvalue gap depends endogenously on the future prevention and absorption investments of downstream agents. Interestingly, greater downstream process reliability increases the continuation-value gaps faced by upstream firms, whereas greater recovery reliability decreases them. We show that liability-only mechanisms with nonnegative transfers cannot implement the first-best outcome once disruption absorption is possible, while natural no-reward/no-penalty benchmarks can be arbitrarily inefficient. To address this limitation, we propose a settlement rule that charges cascading outputs according to their marginal systemic harm and finances successful recovery through absorption credits within a pathwise balanced system. When prevention and absorption technologies follow logit models, the resulting settlement rules can be computed efficiently via a convex dynamic program. Managerial implications: Disruption contracts should distinguish process reliability from recovery reliability and compensate absorbers for the systemic value of successful recovery, rather than merely reimbursing the operational costs incurred during disruption response.

title: How AI Rewrites the Economics of Knowledge Codification

detail.title: How AI Rewrites the Economics of Knowledge Codification
detail.abstract: AI reduces the cost of encoding knowledge into computational artifacts. It does far less to reduce, and often raises, the cost of evaluating, maintaining, and revising what has been encoded. Building on Cowan et al.'s cost-benefit framework, this paper decomposes codification into four capacities (encoding, evaluation, maintenance, revision) and names the resulting shift cost recomposition: AI moves codification cost downstream from encoding rather than removing it. The framework makes explicit a capacity the original model left implicit, revision capacity, the organizational standing to challenge the premises encoded in an artifact, distinct from evaluating its outputs or keeping it current as conditions change. Without revision capacity, organizations accumulate orphaned codification: artifacts whose premises no one can contest. A derived observation refits the framework's temporal premise. When codification rests on an externally controlled substrate (proprietary model weights, generated code, agent configurations built on vendor models and shifting dependencies), the amortization horizon collapses, and the discrete, long-lived investment the original framework assumed becomes a subscription to externally scheduled maintenance. Applied to four codification regimes (supervised machine learning, foundation models, coding agents, agentic systems), the framework identifies three structural patterns: codification moves, unevenly across regimes, from ex ante specification toward runtime generation; authority migrates across organizational actors; and governance mechanisms calibrated for one regime fail to transfer to the next. A dynamic expertise-pipeline extension connects these patterns to the intergenerational reproduction of the expertise that makes codification meaningful, and names an open empirical contribution: the longitudinal study of AI-artifact drift. The framework complements the demand-side and task-substitution accounts now dominant in AI economics with a mechanism grounded in the changing cost of codification itself.

detail.abstract: Generative AI now drafts fluent prose, writes analysis code, and assembles entire manuscripts, yet fluent text is not a credible result. The distance between the two does not shrink as models improve; it grows. This note proposes treating spec-driven development (SDD)-specifications as the source of truth, deterministic builds, and quality gates-not as a writing accelerator but as a governance layer over generative AI in empirical research. We describe an engine for the empirical paper lifecycle in economics and finance in which the manuscript is built from frozen artifacts (design, data, results) rather than written alongside results: numbers enter the text only from analysis outputs, exploration is walled off from confirmation by an explicit design freeze (no-look-ahead), claims are bounded to their evidential status, and every AI action is logged as part of the method (an AI bill of materials). A three-layer survival architecture-epistemic invariants, role-and-gate contracts, and an interchangeable substrate-keeps the method independent of any model or vendor. We name this methodology FSAIM, state precisely what is and is not novel about it, position it against the closest 2025-2026 work, and report its first empirical instance together with that instance's honest shortfalls.

detail.abstract: This study reconceptualises sustainability in peer-to-peer accommodation (P2PA) as a multilevel, practice-based and institutionally embedded process. Existing research has largely adopted consumer-centric and macro-level perspectives, overlooking how sustainability is enacted through everyday hosting practices. Drawing on Social Practice Theory and an institutional perspective, this study conducts a systematic literature review to examine how host sustainability practices are formed, enacted, and transformed. The findings show that sustainability emerges through the dynamic configuration of three interdependent elements-meanings, competences, and materialsrather than from individual attitudes alone. Meanings, rooted in host identity and lifestyle orientations, shape how sustainability is interpreted; competences, developed through learning and social interaction, enable its enactment; and materials, including resource conditions and platform infrastructures, define its feasibility within institutional contexts. The study further demonstrates that sustainability practices are selectively enacted through processes of negotiation and adjustment, reflecting the alignment-or misalignment-of practice elements under structural constraints. Importantly, outcomes such as economic performance, guest experience, and social impact feed back into practice formation, highlighting the recursive and processual nature of sustainability. By advancing a practice-based and institutionally embedded framework, this study makes three key contributions: it shifts sustainability from an attitudinal to a configurational construct; explains the intention-practice gap as a problem of value-practice misalignment; and develops a relational, multi-level understanding of sustainability as co-produced across hosts, platforms, and broader institutional contexts.

title: When Law Slows the Machine: Regulatory Barriers as a Determinant of Automation Risk Across Professions
affiliations: Odesa National University of Technology

detail.title: When Law Slows the Machine: Regulatory Barriers as a Determinant of Automation Risk Across Professions
detail.abstract:
Most models of occupational automation treat regulatory barriers as background noise. This paper argues they are a core variable. We introduce the Regulatory Automation Barrier Index (RABI), a composite metric that quantifies the degree to which a profession's institutional and legal framework delays technological displacement, independent of whether the underlying technology is already capable of performing the work.

The index integrates three dimensions: Licensing Stringency (LS), Legal Exclusivity (LE), and Regulatory Update Frequency (RUF), calculated as RABI = (LS + LE + RUF) / 3. Applied to five occupations across OECD jurisdictions, scores range from 0.10 for warehouse operators to 0.85 for notaries. High-skill professions in law, medicine, and finance face displacement timelines measured in decades rather than years, not because AI cannot perform their functions, but because current law does not permit it.

The paper situates RABI within broader IT market dynamics. Global IT spending reached $5.26 trillion in 2024 and is projected at $6.15 trillion in 2026. Investment in generative AI grew nearly eightfold between 2022 and 2023. Ukraine's IT sector, accounting for 4.9% of GDP and 41.5% of total services exports, serves as a national case study, with a documented structural shift from outsourcing toward product-based development between 2021 and 2023.

The framework has practical implications for workforce planning, education policy, and regulatory design. Whether a job can be automated and whether it will be automated are two different questions, and the gap between them is institutional.

Aukus and Australia's Strategic Autonomy: Security, Deterrence, and Economic Vulnerability in the Indo-Pacific 
A Scholarly Essay in International Relations and Indo-Pacific Security Studies
detail.abstract: Australia has entered a period of strategic transition. For decades, Canberra benefited from a regional order in which economic integration with China could coexist with a security alliance with the United States. The deterioration of Sino-American relations has placed that model under strain. This paper argues that AUKUS marks a departure from Australia's traditional approach to regional security. By committing itself to deeper military integration with the United States and the United Kingdom, Australia has strengthened its capacity to deter coercion in the Indo-Pacific. At the same time, it has increased its exposure to economic pressure from China and reduced its room for diplomatic maneuver. The paper examines the military logic behind AUKUS, the risks associated with economic dependence on China, and the implications of a Taiwan contingency. It also evaluates Australia's relationships with Japan, Indonesia, ASEAN, and the Pacific Islands. The central argument is that Australia's future influence will depend less on military modernization alone than on its ability to reduce strategic vulnerabilities while maintaining constructive relations across the region.

detail.abstract: Purpose-As concerns over climate change and social inequality intensify, firms are increasingly transitioning toward sustainable business models. However, the fragmented nature of the literature limits our understanding of how sustainable transition pathways are constructed. This paper aims to examine how managerial cognition, particularly managers' cognitive frames and their underlying content, influences the construction and efficacy of sustainable transition pathways. Design/methodology/approach-An integrative literature review of 184 studies was conducted using thematic analysis and dialectical interrogation. Findings-Sustainable transition pathways emerge through repeated interventions, shaped by the cognitive frames managers use to guide their decision-making. The authors identify four managerial orientations toward sustainability: business-as-usual, instrumental, transition and transformation, each underpinned by distinct assumptions, values and priorities. These orientations influence how managers conceptualize sustainability, set objectives, operationalize interventions and define value. By integrating these insights, the authors theorize how differences in cognitive content explain variations in the construction and efficacy of sustainable transition pathways. Originality/value-This study uncovers the overlooked role of managerial cognition in shaping sustainable transition pathways by synthesizing the fragmented literature. By identifying differences in cognitive content, the authors develop a conceptual framework of managerial orientations toward sustainability. This framework advances the understanding of how managers construct sustainable transition pathways, explaining why similar interventions can lead to divergent sustainability outcomes. Lastly, this paper offers conceptual insights that can help managers reflect on how to construct more effective sustainable transition pathways.

detail.abstract:
The Green Climate Fund (GCF) was established as a central multilateral vehicle for concessional climate finance, with a mandate to support adaptation in climate-vulnerable countries and mitigation pathways consistent with global climate goals. After a decade of operation, the GCF’s growth raises a structural question that cannot be answered by aggregate approval volumes, average grant shares, or reported leverage alone: is concessional finance being allocated in accordance with structural need?

This paper develops and applies an integrated audit methodology for assessing climate-finance instrument alignment across GCF-approved projects. The methodology combines four ENHANCE Institute frameworks: RFRC™, which defines country-level structural appropriateness of finance; ESF™, which classifies national transition and constraint regimes; C-FAIR™, which evaluates the fit between financing instruments and resilience conditions; and CFAM™, which distinguishes reported leverage from realistic private-capital activation.

Using the GCF portfolio of 352 approved projects from 2015 to March 2026 as an illustrative application, the paper identifies signals of concessionality dilution at scale: grant intensity weakens as project size increases, cross-cutting structures expand, and private-finance channels are applied, even where vulnerable countries remain present in the portfolio. These findings are presented not as a verdict on institutional intent, but as evidence that concessionality requires structural audit rather than aggregate interpretation.

The paper argues that climate-finance concessionality should be assessed against country conditions, instrument fit, vulnerability, and activation feasibility. At the current stage of the climate timeline, the question is no longer whether concessional capital is growing, but whether its structure remains aligned with need.

title: Six Failure Modes of AI Delegation: Deriving the Bounded Agency Primitives from a Feasibility Constraint for Intervention

detail.title: Six Failure Modes of AI Delegation: Deriving the Bounded Agency Primitives from a Feasibility Constraint for Intervention
detail.abstract: The Bounded Agency framework identifies six governance primitives required for institutional control of delegated AI authority. The original formulation (Bhagavatula 2026a) presented these primitives as a governance architecture; this paper derives them from first principles. We begin with a single feasibility constraint: an organization’s capacity to reclaim delegated authority must operate at execution tempo before harm becomes irreversible. On this view, governance is not oversight but the capacity to intervene at the tempo at which a system acts; observation of a deviation that has already propagated is not control. We then enumerate the independent ways this constraint can fail. Each failure mode—unbounded exposure, temporal mismatch, institutional friction, invisible delegation, binary response, and misaligned capacity—defines a necessary condition for intervention feasibility, and each maps to a governance primitive. We demonstrate independence (each failure mode can occur in isolation), argue irreducibility (the six modes cannot be reduced to one another at this level of abstraction), and show that the conjunctive structure of the Bounded Agency Limit follows as a logical consequence rather than a modeling assumption. The derivation reframes the six primitives not as recommended practices but as the minimal set of conditions that must be simultaneously satisfied for delegated AI authority to remain structurally reclaimable.

title: Bounded Agency in the Age of AI: Institutional Foundations and Domain Applications

detail.title: Bounded Agency in the Age of AI: Institutional Foundations and Domain Applications
detail.abstract: AI systems increasingly exercise a range of agencies across critical institutional domains, such as approving loans, moderating content, allocating healthcare resources, and determining benefit eligibility. This paper develops the institutional foundations and domain applications of the Bounded Agency framework introduced in the companion paper, Bhagavatula (2026). While that paper established the six governance primitives (β, τ, λ, ρ, δ, μ), the Bounded Agency Limit (BAL), and the Delegation Factor (DF) as formal governance instruments, this paper explains why the boundary problem arises and how the primitives operate across institutional contexts. Drawing on North's institutional economics, we argue that AI destabilizes the conventional separation between institutions (the rules of the game) and organizations (the players that act within them) through three mechanisms—scale expansion, temporal compression, and compositional opacity—which correspond respectively to failures of accountability mapping (μ), tempo matching (τ), and authority boundary (β). This destabilization is why organizational governance alone is necessary but insufficient: rules written at deliberative tempo cannot bound systems that act at machine tempo. Applying the framework across healthcare, public administration, content platforms, and employment, we show that domain-specific boundary specification is what turns the abstract primitives into enforceable institutional control.

title: Beyond the Charges: What Defense Counsel Rarely Warns You About

detail.title: Beyond the Charges: What Defense Counsel Rarely Warns You About
detail.abstract: Traditional criminal defense practice in Canada operates under a narrow mandate focused primarily on courtroom procedure, evidentiary assessment, and securing legal acquittals. However, for individuals accused within white-collar, regulatory, or non-profit governance contexts, the most devastating punishments often occur long before a formal verdict is delivered. This article examines the critical, systemic "extra-legal" or collateral consequences of criminal allegations that defense counsel routinely fail to anticipate or mitigate. By analyzing the financial realities of crushing legal retainers alongside the rise of arbitrary corporate "de-risking" pipelines by major Canadian financial institutions, this paper exposes how accused individuals are systematically cut off from banking systems and joint family assets. Furthermore, it details the profound mental health tolls multiplied by institutional procedural delays (R. v. Jordan) and the catastrophic reputational fallout suffered by community leaders or unpaid non-profit volunteers. Rejecting the rigid, trial-centric boundaries established in R. v. G.D.B., the author proposes an expanded, holistic standard of care for modern criminal defense. This paper introduces a proactive seven-point "Broader Model of Defense Representation"-spanning risk counseling, resource mapping, and media triage-arguing that true effective assistance of counsel must actively safeguard a client's real-world survival outside the courtroom.

title: CEE-OS: A Computational Evolutionary Economics Operating System for Measuring Structural Fitness, Shock Propagation, and Policy Co-Evolution in the Global Trade Network

detail.title: CEE-OS: A Computational Evolutionary Economics Operating System for Measuring Structural Fitness, Shock Propagation, and Policy Co-Evolution in the Global Trade Network

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No competing interests
declarations.funderStatement: No funding was received for this paper

detail.abstract: Economic performance measurement remains dominated by GDP and its derivatives, which capture aggregate output but fail to reflect a nation's structural capacity to generate, sustain, and adapt economic complexity. We introduce the Computational Evolutionary Economics Operating System (cee-os), a three-layer computational framework that treats national economies as co-evolving agents embedded in a weighted global trade network. Layer 1 constructs the Evolutionary Economic Fitness (eef) index-a multidimensional, dynamical fitness metric computed across 61 countries and 24 years (2000-2023) from World Bank structural indicators spanning information processing, coordination efficiency, adaptive capacity, resource efficiency, innovation, and systemic fragility. Layer 2 implements a network shock propagation engine, calibrated against three historical episodes: the COVID-19 supply shock (2020), the Global Financial Crisis (2008), and the European Energy Crisis (2022). Layer 3 deploys an evolutionary policy simulation in which country-agents co-evolve six-dimensional policy portfolios via trade-weighted social learning and mutation over 500 generations. Three principal findings emerge: eef diverges systematically and meaningfully from GDP per capita, particularly for small open economies and resource-dependent states; shock-induced policy divergence is absorbed by the global trade network's learning dynamics at long time horizons, revealing an attractor-stable policy landscape; and Nash equilibria are unreachable for all 61 agents across all simulation horizons, consistent with rugged fitness landscapes predicted by complexity economics. cee-os provides a reproducible, extensible platform for analysing economic resilience, policy diffusion, and long-run structural change.

title: AI-Driven Decision Making: Is Human Leadership Becoming Obsolete?
affiliations: and National Defence University

detail.title: AI-Driven Decision Making: Is Human Leadership Becoming Obsolete?

detail.abstract: The fast adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) in making decisions in organizations has elicited an increasing controversy about whether human leadership would continue to be relevant in the future. Although AI systems are becoming more efficient, predictive, and based on data, the issues of accountability, ethics, and situational judgment are still present. The fact that AI-based decision-making is transforming the role of a leader (in a way that the issue of a human leader is becoming a thing of the past or simply altering the role of a leader) is critically analyzed in this paper. Resting on the existing research in the domain of AI-human collaboration, the managerial decision-making systems, and the regulation of AI, the paper will combine all the findings on the transformation of leadership roles by AI. It is said that AI will not overturn leadership, but instead convert it into a hybrid model where both people and machines will equally make decisions on the matters. However, limitations in the explainability, ethical reasoning and contextual adaptability makes it still necessary to have humans as lead. The article concludes by saying that the leadership is being transformed into something of a coordination sort of operation where human judgment, emotional intelligence and strategic oversight cannot be overlooked.
