detail.abstract: This study examines the evolving role of Product Ownership in scaling Agile SaaS teams within the European technology ecosystem. Based on secondary research, it explores how Product Owners are transitioning from traditional backlog managers to strategic business enablers. The findings highlight the importance of strategic decisionmaking, stakeholder management, and customer-centric product development in scaled Agile environments. The study also discusses the influence of European market and regulatory factors on Product Ownership practices.

title: Institutional and Regulatory Framework for the Establishment of Real Estate Investment Trusts (REITs): Evidence from the Tanzanian Property Market
affiliations: and American University

detail.title: Institutional and Regulatory Framework for the Establishment of Real Estate Investment Trusts (REITs): Evidence from the Tanzanian Property Market
detail.abstract: This study provides an in-depth assessment of the regulatory and institutional framework governing the establishment and operation of Real Estate Investment Trusts (REITs) in Tanzania. Although REITs were formally introduced under the Capital Markets and Securities framework in 2011 as a mechanism to mobilize long-term capital for real estate development, the market has remained largely underdeveloped. The study employs a qualitative research design drawing on documentary analysis of legislation, regulations, and policy instruments, complemented by stakeholder consultations with regulators, fund managers, and institutional investors. The findings indicate that stringent minimum capital requirements, regulatory complexity, lack of a clear tax pass-through regime, and weak institutional coordination have constrained the development of REITs. A light policy-context update incorporating developments between 2019 and 2024 shows that, despite progress in capital market deepening and housing finance reforms, structural rigidities continue to limit the effectiveness of REITs. The study concludes that targeted regulatory reform, enhanced institutional coordination, and improved tax clarity are essential to unlock the potential of REITs as a sustainable real estate financing vehicle in Tanzania. A peer-reviewed version of this manuscript was published in World Journal of Advanced Research and Reviews, Vol. 29(02), 2026, pp. 616–622

title: Credit Reference Bureaus and Mortgage Performance in Tanzania: Evidence from Commercial Banks
affiliations: and American University

detail.title: Credit Reference Bureaus and Mortgage Performance in Tanzania: Evidence from Commercial Banks
detail.abstract: The introduction of Credit Reference Bureaus (CRBs) in Tanzania was intended to enhance credit risk management, reduce non-performing loans (NPLs), and improve overall credit market performance. While existing literature has extensively examined the role of credit information sharing on general credit outcomes, limited empirical evidence exists on the contribution of CRBs to mortgage performance in Tanzania. This study analyzes the contribution of CRBs to mortgage performance by comparing key performance indicators before and after the adoption of CRBs, assessing the legal and regulatory framework governing CRBs, and evaluating the level of compliance by financial institutions. The study adopts a qualitative case study approach, drawing primary data from semi-structured interviews conducted with senior credit officers, loan officers, and credit analysts from selected commercial banks, as well as operators of licensed Credit Reference Bureaus. Secondary data were obtained from banks' annual reports, regulatory publications, and mortgage market reports issued by the Bank of Tanzania and the Tanzania Mortgage Refinance Company. Data was analyzed using thematic and content analysis techniques. The findings indicate that although mortgage holdings in Tanzania increased at an average rate of approximately 7 percent following the adoption of CRBs, the contribution of CRBs to mortgage performance remains limited. Mortgage non-performing loans continued to rise during the post-adoption period while mortgage returns declined, largely due to persistent data inaccuracies, multiple borrower identification issues, and low confidence among banks in CRB credit reports. The study further finds that financial institutions demonstrate full regulatory compliance with CRB requirements, but structural and legal constraints reduce the effectiveness of CRBs. The study concludes that while CRBs possess significant potential to improve mortgage market performance in Tanzania, their impact remains constrained by regulatory gaps and operational challenges. Policy recommendations include strengthening the legal framework governing CRBs, improving data accuracy and borrower identification systems, and enhancing supervisory support to improve the effectiveness of credit information sharing. A peer-reviewed version of this manuscript was published in World Journal of Advanced Research and Reviews, Vol. 29(02), 2026, pp. 616–622.

title: Which Coherent Corner? An Options Appraisal for Europe's Stablecoin Choice

detail.title: Which Coherent Corner? An Options Appraisal for Europe's Stablecoin Choice
detail.abstract: Europe's 2026 review of MiCA is usually framed as one choice for the euro stablecoin. The real question is the mix. A trilemma-par stability, private credit, no public backstop-lets a single token hold only two of the three; the corner that reaches for all three is structurally unstable, for reasons of coordination that no calibration fixes. But at the level of the system the three coherent designs are not rivals: they are lanes that can run in parallel-narrow money (a privately issued claim on the central bank), bank money (bank-issued tokens and tokenised deposits), and a public anchor (a digital euro and on-chain central-bank money). This note weighs each against six EU objectives, shows that the best mix turns on which objectives are prioritised, and offers a conditional sequenced portfolio-with one unconditional conclusion: close the incoherent non-bank corner.

title: Money or Credit? MiCA's Stablecoin Hybrid and the Direction of the 2026 Review

detail.title: Money or Credit? MiCA's Stablecoin Hybrid and the Direction of the 2026 Review
detail.abstract: Are stablecoins a new kind of money, or a new kind of bank? Europe's Markets in Crypto-Assets Regulation (MiCA) has never quite decided. It treats a fiat-backed stablecoin-an "e-money token"-as a digital wrapper around existing money, yet loads the issuer with much of a bank's prudential machinery. The result is coherent in one case and unstable in another, depending on who issues it. A bank-issued token sits inside the public safety net, and the arrangement holds. A non-bank issuer faces the same bank-grade rules but no safety net-an instrument that promises to be worth one euro, invests in assets that can lose value, and has nothing to fall back on in a panic. Those three features cannot all hold at once. Reading the 2026 review consultation as a live document, the note finds three EU institutions pulling this corner three ways, and argues the review should choose one coherent design, not fine-tune an incoherent middle.

title: What the Rule-Book Cannot See: Codified Doctrine, the Epistemic Immune System, and the Distribution of Supervisory Attention

detail.title: What the Rule-Book Cannot See: Codified Doctrine, the Epistemic Immune System, and the Distribution of Supervisory Attention

declarations.declarationOfInterest: This was an independent study and I have no relationships to any person or organization that would influence this study.
declarations.funderStatement: I have funded this research personally.

detail.abstract: The endogenous-money debate is settled operationally: central banks set the price of reserves and accommodate the quantity, as the post-Keynesian literature argued and the Bank of England's 2014 account states publicly. Yet the codified rule-book — Basel risk-weights, the legal definition of money, stress-test taxonomies, the mandate — was written on opposite, veil-view assumptions and not rewritten. What does that lag do to supervision? Codified categories, the paper argues, shape the surveillance regime: a category-system makes some risks countable and others unrepresentable, so codified doctrine works as an epistemic immune system, specialised against the prior crisis and blind to risks of a different kind. Doctrine does not decide which settlement is codified — material interests and path dependence do that; the contribution is downstream, in the sociology of ignorance. It separates doctrinal blindness, where a risk has no category, from motivated blindness, where a recognised risk goes unwatched because a coalition benefits, distinguished in the record by a missing versus a suppressed category. The dependent variable, the distribution of supervisory attention, has four observable proxies. The mechanism is shown in three historical episodes and a set of contemporary gaps; a discriminating archival case — Competition and Credit Control 1971 and the Secondary Banking Crisis — is specified for a companion paper.

title: Health-Care Transformation in Brazil’s Unified Health System at 35 Years: Innovations, Achievements, Persistent Challenges, and Future Directions
affiliations: Getulio Vargas Foundation (FGV) - Sao Paulo School of Business Administration, Getulio Vargas Foundation (FGV) - Sao Paulo School of Business Administration, Fundação Oswaldo Cruz and

detail.title: Health-Care Transformation in Brazil’s Unified Health System at 35 Years: Innovations, Achievements, Persistent Challenges, and Future Directions

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no competing interests.
declarations.funderStatement: Andreza Davidian receives funding from the São Paulo Research Foundation (FAPESP) under grant number 2025/06974-40.

detail.abstract:
Background: Brazil's Unified Health System (Sistema Único de Saúde, SUS) is one of the world's largest universal public health systems. Over its first 35 years it expanded access at every level of care, yet the transformation of the underlying model of care advanced unevenly across primary, specialised outpatient, and hospital care. We examined how this expansion reshaped the organisation of care and why its trajectories diverged.

Methods: We conducted a historically informed, policy-oriented analysis of the SUS model of care, combining selected quantitative indicators from national administrative systems (CNES, SIA/SUS, SIH/SUS, and SAGE) with a descriptive-analytical examination of policy instruments, financing mechanisms, and provision arrangements across primary care, specialised outpatient care, and hospital care. These components were assessed through three cross-cutting dimensions: patterns of expansion and organisation, mechanisms of induction, and structural constraints on integration.

Findings: All three components expanded substantially, but transformation of the model of care was greatest where a financing instrument capable of inducing change was joined to an explicit project to reorganise provision. Primary care moved furthest, building a territorial, population-based model linked to gains in health outcomes and equity. Hospital care changed the least, its institutional environment reformed far more than its clinical core. Specialised outpatient care expanded faster yet remained the most fragmented, organised around the procedure rather than the care pathway.

Interpretation: Expanding access and transforming the model of care are distinct achievements; consolidating an integrated, equitable model remains the central challenge for the SUS and for universal systems pursuing the same goal.

title: Prevalence and Determinants of Steatotic Liver Disease among Patients with Diabetes in Rural Uganda

detail.title: Prevalence and Determinants of Steatotic Liver Disease among Patients with Diabetes in Rural Uganda

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no conflicts of interest
declarations.ethicsApproval: The study was approved by the Ethics Committee of St. Mary's Hospital Lacor (Gulu) (LACOR-2024-329 -approval number) and registered with the Uganda National Council for Science and Technology (HS4585ES -UNCST-registration number). All participants provided written informed consent. All data were anonymized and handled confidentially.
declarations.funderStatement: This study received unrestricted funding from the Associazione per la Ricerca Gastroenterologica Roberto Farini and the Rotary Club Padova.

detail.abstract:
Background: Data on steatotic liver disease (SLD) among diabetic patients in rural Sub-Saharan Africa are scarce. Understanding its burden and metabolic correlates is essential in regions undergoing early nutrition and lifestyle transition.

Methods: We conducted a cross-sectional study among 176 adults at St. John XXIII Hospital in Aber, Northern Uganda. Sociodemographic, clinical, laboratory, lifestyle, and dietary data were collected. Hepatic steatosis was assessed by semi-quantitative ultrasound. Dietary patterns were analysed using a food-frequency questionnaire and principal component analysis (PCA). Multivariate logistic regression identified factors associated with SLD.

Findings: SLD was detected in 24% of the 176 participants enrolled. Most cases (76%) were consistent with pure metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD), while viral hepatitis and alcohol contributed to a minority. Patients with SLD were older, more often male, overweight or obese, had higher blood pressure, and lower non-occupational physical activity (all p <0·05). Male sex, waist circumference, and metformin use were independent predictors of SLD. Moderate-to-severe steatosis was associated with higher intake of meat and animal-source proteins. PCA identified dietary patterns reflecting early nutrition transition, with coexistence of traditional plant-based diets and increasing consumption of energy-dense, animal-source foods.

Interpretation: SLD represents a relevant comorbidity among diabetic patients in this rural Ugandan setting, reflecting early lifestyle westernisation. Despite a lower-than-expected prevalence, strong associations with metabolic risk factors highlight the need to integrate liver assessment into diabetes care, with emphasis on lifestyle interventions in low-resource settings.

title: How Digitalization Drives Improvements in the Effects of Government Green Intervention: Considering the Impact of Agent Attributes
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: How Digitalization Drives Improvements in the Effects of Government Green Intervention: Considering the Impact of Agent Attributes
detail.abstract: Government interventions aimed at addressing market failures often face the dilemma of information asymmetry, while digitalization enables more precise government intervention. This study explores how big data can be utilized to improve the effectiveness of government intervention in industrial green development. The effects of government green intervention (GGI) are categorized into two types: the structural effect (the greening of the industrial structure) and the intensity effect (the enhancement of green total factor productivity). Based on both theoretical analysis and empirical research in China, this study demonstrates that digitalization enhances both the structural and intensity effects of green intervention, fostering synergy between greening and development. Furthermore, the influence of agent attributes on the effects of GGI is examined. The results indicate that in regions with strong agent attributes, digitalization has a weaker impact on improving the structural effect of intervention but a stronger impact on enhancing the intensity effect. These findings facilitate a shift in GGI from administrative interference to market-based indirect tools.

title: Networks of Change: Infrastructure and Steam Diffusion in 19th-Century France
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, University of Strasbourg and University of Cambridge

detail.title: Networks of Change: Infrastructure and Steam Diffusion in 19th-Century France
detail.abstract: This paper examines how transport infrastructure shaped the diffusion of steam power across French departments between 1840 and 1911. Using a newly constructed annual departmental panel of steam engine stocks, firms, and installed horsepower, we reconstruct regional diffusion trajectories and estimate the causal impact of transport connectivity on mechanization. We combine department and year fixed effects with an instrumental-variable strategy based on successive French railway planning laws to address the endogeneity of railway expansion.The results reveal substantial territorial heterogeneity in the timing and speed of adoption, indicating that industrialization unfolded unevenly across space. Railway expansion exerted a positive and increasingly strong effect on steam adoption from the mid-1860s onward. An additional 100 kilometers of railway is associated with roughly six additional steam engines per 10,000 inhabitants around 1865 and more than nine by 1900. Navigable waterways also promoted adoption, though their role evolved from complementing railways to becoming progressively substituted by them as the rail network matured.To identify the mechanisms underlying these effects, we construct time-varying measures of accessibility to coal markets and engineering expertise. The results indicate that improved access to coal significantly increased steam adoption throughout the second half of the nineteenth century, while access to engineering knowledge became important only in the 1890s as steam technology grew more complex. The findings suggest that the diffusion of general-purpose technologies depended not only on relative prices and local endowments but also on the infrastructures that reduced economic and informational frictions across space.

title: Don’t Give Up on Lab Experiments: Why the Field Still Needs the Lab
affiliations: University of Chicago - Department of Economics

detail.title: Don’t Give Up on Lab Experiments: Why the Field Still Needs the Lab
detail.abstract:
Recent enthusiasm for field experiments, and especially for natural field experiments (NFEs), in which subjects go about their daily activities unaware that any study is taking place, has sometimes been read as a verdict against the laboratory. I argue that such a verdict is wrong. Through the lens of a simple rational-choice model, I show that the four standard experimental designs (laboratory, artefactual field experiment (AFE), framed field experiment (FFE), and NFE) are comparative-static restrictions of one maximization problem, each identifying a parameter the others cannot. The model reveals that each design type has distinctive strengths and weaknesses across various dimensions of knowledge creation, including the enforcement of the conditions for causal identification, the faithfulness of the experimental environment to the theory being tested, the identification of economic primitives via theoretical structure, and the ethics of studying human subjects. On each of the dimensions, the four design types are complements rather than rivals. Nowhere is this complementarity more evident than between the two extremes. The lab enforces the conditions for causal identification that the NFE must inherit from the market; the NFE recovers the parameter that governs behaviour in the wild, free of the selection, scrutiny, and environmental distortions the lab cannot escape. A research programme using all four designs together demonstrates something no single design can produce. The framework further accommodates the recent rise of online and survey experiments as natural extensions. Our discipline’s recent drift away from laboratory evidence is leaving an important structural gap that natural field experiments, however well conceived, cannot fill.

title: Blindly Discriminating: The GI Bill and Racial Inequality
affiliations: Stanford University and

detail.title: Blindly Discriminating: The GI Bill and Racial Inequality
detail.abstract:
The World War II GI Bill was the largest education subsidy in US history and a cornerstone of the postwar US transition to a knowledge economy. Although formally race-blind, the program's decentralized administration left implementation to local officials and segregated institutions, with sharply different consequences for Black and white veterans. This paper quantifies the GI Bill's impact on Black and white Americans' economic outcomes across two generations, using a regression discontinuity around WWII service eligibility cutoffs and a new data linkage from veterans in the 1940 and 1950 censuses to their sons' neighborhood outcomes between 1990 and 2025. The GI Bill widened racial inequality, doubling white veterans' college completion while steering Black veterans into often-fraudulent vocational programs with no earnings returns. The disparities persisted across generations, increasing the white-Black gap in sons' adult-neighborhood outcomes, including a 5-percentage-point (47 percent) widening of the racial college gap. Unequal returns to the same eligibility account for the intergenerational gap, with no contribution from prewar differences in socioeconomic status or geography. In sum, access to the GI Bill was not nearly the same economic opportunity for Black Americans as it was for white Americans, highlighting that race-blind policy does not guarantee racial equality.

title: On the Physics of Expected Asset Returns
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: On the Physics of Expected Asset Returns

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study does not involve human participants, patients, or case studies requiring ethics approval. All data used are publicly available.
declarations.funderStatement: This research was conducted independently, without external funding or institutional support.

detail.abstract: A central tension in asset pricing has gone unresolved for six decades: the efficient-market hypothesis implies that excess returns should be competed away, yet they persist. Grossman and Stiglitz showed that perfectly efficient prices are impossible and posited an "equilibrium degree of disequilibrium," but left its magnitude and permanence asserted rather than derived. This paper supplies the missing structure. It factors the expected gross return of any asset into two independent primitives, a long-term structural compounding baseline (c_t) and a short-term temporal elasticity (K_t,T), as a geometric identity requiring no assumptions about cash flows, utility, or equilibrium. From this decomposition, integrating an exponential dispersion law gives the Asset Opportunity Space (AOS), a closed-form bound Omega_t = eta|c_t|/lambda on the exploitable expectational displacement in an asset. The AOS quantifies the Grossman-Stiglitz residual exactly and shows it to be permanent on three independent grounds: physically, arbitrage takes finite time; geometrically, heterogeneous observers cannot be reconciled by any single trade; and epistemologically, forecasting disagreement is irreducible while the future is uncertain. In the spirit of Shannon's channel capacity, the AOS bounds what is available to all participants without prescribing the strategy that realizes it. The same decomposition yields a Relativity Theorem (the AOS is observer-dependent, with an invariant fingerprint (lambda, R-squared, eta_0, Omega_0) common to all constant baselines), recasts equilibrium models as normative coordination devices, and is structurally isomorphic to mass-energy equivalence (Omega = |c| eta/lambda, analogous to E = mc-squared). Empirically, across U.S. equities, gold, and Bitcoin the decay law holds with R-squared up to 0.86, and Bitcoin's peak AOS falls from roughly 625 to below 80 units across successive cycles as institutional maturation raises efficiency.

title: Monopsony Power and the Transmission of Monetary Policy
affiliations: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, University of Pennsylvania and The Wharton School, University of Pennsylvania

detail.title: Monopsony Power and the Transmission of Monetary Policy
detail.abstract:
This paper studies how labor market power affects the transmission of monetary policy. Using administrative U.S. Census data, we show that firms with high monopsony power—defined as those accounting for over 10 percent of the local wage bill—respond less to monetary policy in terms of their wage bill and employment. We then develop a New Keynesian model with heterogeneous firms and oligopsonistic competition to interpret these findings. Wage stickiness combined with firms’ labor market power is key to generating the heterogeneous responses that we document. Our model highlights two channels through which oligopsony shapes the aggregate effects of monetary policy: partial passthrough and misallocation. Calibrated to U.S. labor markets, the model implies that the decline in labor market power since the 1980s has increased the output response to monetary policy by about 10 percent and accounts for about 15 percent of the estimated flattening of the Phillips curve.

title: Anchored Expectations and Machine Learning Intermediaries: Forecasting Indian CPI Inflation in the Post-FIT Regime

detail.title: Anchored Expectations and Machine Learning Intermediaries: Forecasting Indian CPI Inflation in the Post-FIT Regime
detail.abstract: India's formal adoption of Flexible Inflation Targeting (FIT) in 2016 fundamentally altered the structural data-generating process of CPI inflation, shifting it from a self-reinforcing unanchored process to a mean-reverting one gravitating toward the 4% target. This paper evaluates five model architectures, ARIMA, ARIMAX, XGBoost, Elastic Net, and an ARIMA-XGBoost hybrid, against a 52-month expanding window walk-forward validation spanning January 2022 to April 2026. ARIMA(3,0,0) achieves the best RMSE of 0.7024, confirming that post-2016 Indian inflation is fundamentally momentum-driven. The ARIMA-XGBoost hybrid achieves the best MAE of 0.5316, with the Diebold-Mariano test confirming no statistically significant difference between the two (DM statistic:-0.08, p-value: 0.94). SHAP decomposition independently identifies M3 broad money with a 12-month transmission lag as the fourth most important predictor , confirming through a machine learning lens the monetary transmission channel previously established via VECM cointegration analysis. Time-varying SHAP contributions reveal CPI lag 1 transitioning from self-reinforcing pre-2016 to mean-reverting post-2016, providing direct algorithmic evidence of the structural anchor introduced by FIT.

title: India's Emerging Geoeconomic Architecture and the Pursuit of Strategic Sovereignty
affiliations: Indian Institute of Information Technology Lucknow

detail.title: India's Emerging Geoeconomic Architecture and the Pursuit of Strategic Sovereignty
detail.abstract: This paper explores how India has evolved from a passive participant in global trade to a crucial geoeconomic player that's actively pursuing strategic sovereignty in the face of growing trade fragmentation. By analysing data from the International Monetary Fund (IMF) Article IV consultations and focusing on three key areas-proactive industrial policies through Production Linked Incentive (PLI) schemes, digital public infrastructure (DPI) as a diplomatic asset, and strategic trade diversification-we illustrate how India is capitalizing on its domestic market size to reduce risks associated with weaponized interdependence while still achieving impressive growth. Our analysis shows that India's strategic engagement, rather than retreating into isolation, positions it to sustain a GDP growth rate of 6.6-7.3 percent through 2027, despite anticipated tariff shocks. By March 2025, India's PLI initiatives had drawn in ₹1.76 lakh crore ($21 billion) in investments across 14 sectors, leading to over ₹16.5 lakh crore ($191 billion) in production and the creation of 1.2 million jobs. Additionally, India's Unified Payments Interface (UPI) has emerged as the largest realtime payment system globally, handling over 250 billion transactions annually worth $3.4 trillion, which accounts for 50 percent of the world's digital transaction volume. These insights suggest that India's strategy could serve as a practical model for other emerging economies trying to navigate the complexities of great power competition while keeping their macroeconomic stability intact.

detail.abstract: Revised Version III integrates the original monographic JMLPI architecture with the calibrated second draft. Rather than claiming an unconditional closure of the open problem, we give a solution architecture for a restricted conditional version: a four-layer Bayesian inference programme which becomes statistically coherent and computationally tractable under three explicit assumption clusters. Our contribution is a reduction of the open problem to independently testable sub-problems, with one fully specified combinatorial kernel and several higher-level geometric, topological and epidemiological extensions stated as conditional, diagnostic, or conjectural. Our central positive result is a tree-sequence/Rao–Blackwell cache-invalidation theorem: after a breakpoint move, geographic likelihood messages need be recomputed only on an explicit upward/downward dependency boundary of a maximumagreement-forest footprint. We stratify the remaining layers–adaptive epidemiological priors, Wasserstein posterior coherence, sheaf-theoretic obstruction summaries, Fisher–Rao curvature diagnostics, identifiability, NPA audit, and Lean formalisation–by proof status and falsification criteria. We include a reproducible toy benchmark, a technical supplement and a slide deck so that the computational and expository claims are inspectable as repository artefacts rather than merely asserted in prose.

title: Measuring Financial Literacy with the Big Three: Why It Works

detail.title: Measuring Financial Literacy with the Big Three: Why It Works
detail.abstract:
This paper investigates why the widely-used Big Three financial literacy index provides a reliable measure of financial literacy. Using an Item Response Theory framework, we estimate item difficulty and discrimination parameters and conduct a meta analysis to assess the stability of these properties across datasets and countries. Results confirm the scale's validity and reliability, with item characteristics that remain stable across populations and settings. We find no evidence of measurement differences across demographic subgroups or countries. Compared to the longer Big Five scale, the Big Three index performs similarly in measuring financial literacy and predicting financial behaviors.

title: Crystallised Ownership Framework (COF) A Pre-Custodial Fractional Programmable Ownership Architecture for Productive Assets
affiliations: and

detail.title: Crystallised Ownership Framework (COF) A Pre-Custodial Fractional Programmable Ownership Architecture for Productive Assets
detail.abstract: The Crystallized Ownership Framework (COF) proposes a pre-custodial architecture for programmable claims associated with productive real-world assets. The framework addresses a recurring problem in asset tokenization: the tendency to conflate a tradable digital instrument with ownership, custody, registry recognition, or legal finality. COF separates these layers by treating programmable claim instruments as conditional economic and procedural claims rather than continuous representations of asset title. Under COF, ownership or enforceable participation does not arise from issuance, possession, or transfer of a claim instrument. Instead, ownership finality is designed to crystallize only through an explicit redemption process, irreversible burn or extinguishment of the relevant claim, and any required off-chain recognition by a registry, custodian, operator, trustee, contract, or other authority. This redeem-to-own architecture permits claim liquidity while preserving a boundary between market activity and ownership formation. The framework is particularly suited to productive assets such as renewable energy generation, battery storage, grid services, net-zero real estate, and infrastructure assets, where value is generated through physical operation and measurable service delivery rather than speculative price appreciation alone. By defining ownership as a discrete crystallized outcome rather than a continuously mirrored token state, COF offers a technology-neutral reference architecture for institutional design, policy analysis, and implementation planning. This paper formalizes COF through core definitions, claim states, lifecycle events, and implementation invariants. It also distinguishes COF from custodial tokenization models and clarifies that legal classification remains jurisdiction-and implementation-specific. The contribution of COF is not to replace existing legal registries or custodial systems, but to provide a structural method for separating programmable claim circulation from ownership finality in digital asset architectures.

title: On the training of physics-informed neural operators for solving parametric partial differential equations
affiliations: Tongji University, University of Oxford, Tongji University, Yale University and Tongji University

detail.title: On the training of physics-informed neural operators for solving parametric partial differential equations

keywords.keywords: Neural operators \and Physics-informed machine learning \and  Partial differential equations

detail.abstract: Physics-informed neural operators (PINOs) aim to learn solution operators for partial differential equations by using the governing physics as supervision, rather than relying solely on paired input-output simulation data. By incorporating physical constraints into the training objective, PINOs combine the cross-instance generalization of neural operators with the data efficiency of physics-informed learning. Despite this promise, how to train PINOs efficiently and robustly remains less well-understood than the training of either data-driven neural operators or physics-informed neural networks (PINNs).To bridge this gap, we examine key components of the PINO training pipeline, including architecture design, optimizer choice, loss balancing, and collocation-point sampling strategy. We study three representative operator backbones, Deep Operator Network (DeepONet), Fourier Neural Operator (FNO), and Continuous Vision Transformer (CViT), across five diverse parametric PDE systems. Our results show that CViT provides consistently strong and stable performance across the considered benchmarks.Beyond architecture, we find that several optimization pathologies previously identified in PINN training naturally arise in PINOs, including gradient conflicts and causal violation. We also find that mitigation algorithms developed for PINNs remain effective in the PINO setting. We further compare physics-informed and data-driven training under different data regimes, revealing that a carefully designed physics-informed training pipeline can match, and in some cases, outperform purely data-driven neural operators.Taken together, these findings provide a systematic empirical understanding of the optimization challenges in PINO training and inform a practical pipeline for efficient and robust physics-informed operator learning. Code and data are publicly available at \url{https://github.com/NanxiiChen/PI-CViT}.

title: Human Factors in UAV Adoption for Logistics: A Multiple Case Study Investigation
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, Polytechnic University of Milan, Saarland University, affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Human Factors in UAV Adoption for Logistics: A Multiple Case Study Investigation
detail.abstract: Unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) offer significant economic, environmental, and labor-saving benefits for logistics. However, human factors (HF) remain underexplored. To address this gap, this study utilized multiple case studies and semi-structured interviews with companies implementing UAVs in logistics to examine HF impacts by adopting a human-centric perspective.,The results validate the advantages of UAVs and identify key HF that support successful adoption. Unlike previous research, findings reveal that UAV noise is generally indistinguishable from urban background sounds, posing minimal annoyance. Effective UAV integration requires targeted training to help operators adapt and ensure safe, efficient use.,Delegating hazardous tasks to technology improves physical and psychosocial well-being, enabling individuals to focus on monitoring and analysis, thereby increasing job satisfaction. Furthermore, the research highlights early stakeholder engagement to enhance technology acceptance and recommends that academia offer practical UAV integration experiences, informed by ten case studies involving both technology users and providers.

title: Magnaporthiopsis paspali associated with root disease of seashore paspalum in Hainan, China

detail.title: Magnaporthiopsis paspali associated with root disease of seashore paspalum in Hainan, China
detail.abstract: Seashore paspalum (Paspalum vaginatum Swartz) is a preferred turfgrass species for golf courses in coastal regions of China. In autumn 2021, patch disease symptoms were observed on seashore paspalum (Paspalum vaginatum Swartz) fairways at several golf courses in Hainan province, China. Fungal isolates with consistent morphological characteristics were recovered from discolored root tissues. Three representative isolates were selected for comprehensive identification based on morphological features and multi-locus phylogenetic analyses. Phylogenetic trees were constructed using maximum likelihood and Bayesian inference of ITS, SSU, LSU, MCM7, RPB1, and TEF1α sequences revealed that the isolates formed a distinct and well-supported clade within the genus Magnaporthiopsis, consistent with their unique morphological traits. Pathogenicity tests demonstrated that the fungus colonizes seashore paspalum roots through ectotrophic dark runner hyphae, casuing to root discoloration, reductions in root and shoot biomass, and leaf chlorosis. Based on morphological, phylogenetic, and pathogenic characteristics, a new species, Magnaporthiopsis paspali, is proposed as the causal agent of root disease in seashore paspalum. In vitro assays showed that propiconazole, benzovindiflupyr, and fluazinam significantly inhibited the mycelial growth of M. paspali, indicating that their potential for effective disease management in field.

title:
Dissociative Recombination: 
2014 Hukou Reform and Internal Migration Patterns in China

detail.title:
Dissociative Recombination: 
2014 Hukou Reform and Internal Migration Patterns in China
detail.abstract: Hukou system in China is a mandatory registration scheme that ties access to social benefits with registration address, and prevents ruralto-urban migration. In 2014, the State Council in China introduced differentiated hukou policies across cities by population size, relaxing most hukou requirements in cities with a population of less than three million. Using a two-way fixed-effects difference-indifferences design model, this paper analyses to the China Migrants Dynamic Survey (CMDS) data to examine whether the reform raised migrants' willingness to settle in small and medium cities. Following the reform, migrants report a 5 percentage point increase in willingness to reside in small and medium cities in the long term, after controlling for individual characteristics and year and city fixed effects. This settlement effect concentrates in cities below 3 million, where the reform granted full relaxation of registration requirements. The findings suggest that loosening residential barriers can redirect long-run migration flows away from megacities, with direct implications for China's urban-rural integration and economic policies.

title: Economic Assimilation of Women and Families in the Age of Mass Migration
affiliations: Australian National University (ANU)

detail.title: Economic Assimilation of Women and Families in the Age of Mass Migration
detail.abstract:
During the Age of Mass Migration, over forty percent of immigrants were women, yet most research focuses on men. Using linked 1900 and 1910 Census records, I show that economic assimilation patterns differed for men and women, and families assimilated at different rates than individuals. Immigrant families improved their relative income scores compared with US-born families, driven by reliance on multiple earners, particularly women’s and children’s labor. At the individual level, gaps between immigrant and US-born income scores were larger for women than men, and the gap for women barely changed even after twenty years of stay.

title: Automation and Repression
affiliations: Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) - Department of Economics, Bilkent University and University of North Carolina (UNC) at Chapel Hill - Department of Public Policy

detail.title: Automation and Repression
detail.abstract:
We consider a model of automation embedded in a political environment where workers can undertake a revolt (modeled as a global game), and greater inequality between capital and labor increases the likelihood of a revolt. Decentralized automation decisions raise the share of capital in national income and increase the likelihood of a successful revolt. A capitalist state (representing capital-owners) prefers to regulate the level of automation to lessen the threat of a successful revolt. The capitalist state can also redistribute to workers via the tax system or repress political action, thus creating greater room for further automation. We characterize the trade-off between the regulation of automation, redistribution and repression. Our main result is a complementarity between automation and repression. Unless the threat of revolt is quite weak or the capital stock is very low, the capitalist state prefers repression. A higher capital stock in turn encourages more automation and thus more repression. In our full dynamic model with capital accumulation, in the long run the economy tends to repression (again unless the threat of revolt is very weak). We also prove that the same conclusions apply when firms can additionally invest in new labor-intensive tasks. Finally, we show that, starting in a democracy, capital accumulation and thus greater automation encourages the capitalists to support a coup against democracy and set up a repressive system.

title: Demographic Divergence: The Legacy of the Opioid Epidemic
affiliations: University of Toronto, University of Notre Dame and University of Toronto

detail.title: Demographic Divergence: The Legacy of the Opioid Epidemic
detail.abstract:
We study how the opioid epidemic shaped local population dynamics in the United States. Exploiting variation in exposure that stems from Purdue Pharma's targeted marketing of OxyContin to high-cancer-mortality areas, we find that more exposed commuting zones experienced lower population growth. By 2020, a one-standard-deviation increase in exposure reduced population growth among individuals aged 18 to 64 by 2.4 percentage points. Direct mortality from drug-induced deaths made only a limited contribution to these changes. Instead, population losses were primarily driven by migratory responses: exposure increased out-migration rates, especially among college-educated individuals. These responses are consistent with the opioid epidemic operating as a disamenity shock, deteriorating local quality of life. Working in the opposite direction, we also document a rise in fertility rates that, by 2020, partially counteracts these population losses. Our findings show that the opioid epidemic reshaped local demographic composition and contributed to the long-run divergence in population dynamics across U.S. commuting zones.

title: The Targets of Geoeconomic Coercion
affiliations: Yale School of Management, Stanford Graduate School of Business and Columbia University - Columbia Business School, Economics

detail.title: The Targets of Geoeconomic Coercion
detail.abstract:
Great powers, like the United States and China, use existing trade and financial linkages of their economies to the rest of the world to exert geoeconomic power. The targeted entities include both foreign governments and foreign private firms. We characterize conditions under which a hegemonic country optimally targets private entities or their government in a given targeted foreign country. An advantage of coercing private entities is that they internalize less than their own government the equilibrium consequences of acquiescing to the hegemon's coercion. This allows the hegemon to build its power by exploiting the difference between the private cost to the targeted entity of the costly actions it demands and the social value to the hegemon of those actions. Coercing the government gives up some of this advantage, but offers the ability of having the targeted government potentially influence firms in its domestic economy that the hegemon finds valuable to coerce but for which it had limited direct coercive power. The relative strength of these two channels determines the optimal mix of coercion targeted at private entities and governments.

detail.abstract: This paper describes the implementation of social annotation activities using Perusall across three upper-level economics courses over six semesters. Students were provided with a framework for reading empirical economics papers and completed weekly collaborative annotations. The framework builds on existing pedagogical approaches but expands them to address elements particularly important in upper-level economics courses: applying theoretical foundations, identifying heterogeneity in results, evaluating mechanisms, and connecting findings to policy implications. Implementation across undergraduate courses such as Development Economics, Economics of Global Poverty, and Women in Economics demonstrates the framework's flexibility across different substantive areas. Observations suggest sustained student engagement throughout the semester, improved quality of classroom discussions, and students' increased ability to connect concepts across readings. The paper provides detailed guidance on assignment design, reading selection, and practical implementation for instructors interested in adopting similar approaches.

detail.abstract: Municipal waste systems in the United States are entering a second stage of policy pressure. The first stage was defined by the expansion of mandates: organics diversion, landfill methane monitoring, packaging extended producer responsibility, disposal bans, and increasingly formal reporting requirements. The second stage is now defined by whether cities can operationalize those requirements through measurement systems, processing infrastructure, procurement design, and localized recovery capacity. Drawing on Climate Systems Insider Issues 5-8 and the Municipal Waste Systems OS research model, this paper identifies four connected shifts: measurement is becoming infrastructure; organics collection is expanding faster than processing capacity; deferred system costs are surfacing as rate, procurement, and compliance risk; and distributed organics models are becoming a practical response to centralized capacity constraints.

title: Gulf Sovereign Wealth Fund Repositioning Amid the 2026 US-Iran Conflict: Transmission Channels to Pakistan's External Account and Policy Imperatives

detail.title: Gulf Sovereign Wealth Fund Repositioning Amid the 2026 US-Iran Conflict: Transmission Channels to Pakistan's External Account and Policy Imperatives
detail.abstract: The 2026 US-Iran war, triggered by Operation Epic Fury on 28 February 2026, has precipitated the most severe global energy security crisis in recorded history. The effective closure of the Strait of Hormuzthrough which approximately 20 per cent of global oil trade transits-has destabilised Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) economies, forcing sovereign wealth funds (SWFs) of ADIA, PIF, QIA, Mubadala, and ADQ to defensively reposition global portfolios. This paper analyses how SWF capital repositioning and GCC economic contraction transmit to Pakistan's external account through three principal channels: energy import costs, remittance compression, and trade finance disruption. Drawing on SEC EDGAR 13D/13G filing data and macroeconomic indicators, the paper demonstrates that Pakistan-identified by S&P Global as the most vulnerable Asia-Pacific economy to this conflict-faces a compound external shock threatening IMF programme continuity. The paper concludes with targeted policy recommendations for Pakistan's Ministry of Finance, State Bank of Pakistan, and Ministry of Commerce.

title: The Luevano Standard: Engineering Algorithmic Consistency as a Prerequisite for Institutional Runtime Authority

detail.title: The Luevano Standard: Engineering Algorithmic Consistency as a Prerequisite for Institutional Runtime Authority
detail.abstract: High-risk automated systems — those governing access to employment, credit, housing, healthcare, and public benefits — currently operate under a regime of probabilistic risk management that is structurally inadequate to prevent, detect, or remedy algorithmic discrimination. This article proposes the Luevano Standard, a civil-rights-grounded governance framework requiring that high-risk automated systems satisfy three architectural prerequisites before deployment: (1) runtime enforcement of machine-readable Normative Constraints derived from anti-discrimination law; (2) Glass-Box transparency producing Auditable Reasoning Traces linked to every consequential decision; and (3) cryptographically unforgeable decision records creating a non-repudiable chain of accountability. The Standard is grounded in the legal logic of Luevano v. Campbell (D.D.C. 1981) and its progeny, which established that opaque, probabilistic selection devices that produce disparate impact cannot satisfy anti-discrimination obligations without transparent validation and structural accountability. The article argues that today's algorithmic selection devices replicate the structural defects of the Professional and Administrative Career Examination (PACE) challenged in Luevano — at vastly greater scale and opacity — and that the same doctrinal logic that dismantled the PACE exam demands the architectural transformation proposed here. The article situates the Luevano Standard within the existing regulatory landscape of the NIST AI Risk Management Framework and the EU AI Act, arguing that the Standard extends and hardens these risk-based approaches by making civil-rights compliance a verifiable architectural condition rather than a probabilistic aspiration.

title: Economic Diversification in Saudi Arabia: The Role of Oil Rents, FDI, and Vision 2030

detail.title: Economic Diversification in Saudi Arabia: The Role of Oil Rents, FDI, and Vision 2030
detail.abstract: This paper examines the impact of oil rents, Foreign Direct Investment (FDI), and the Vision 2030 reform programme on economic diversification in Saudi Arabia over the period 1990-2021. Using time-series econometric methods-including OLS with HAC (Newey-West) standard errors, interaction analysis, and Instrumental Variable (IV) estimation via 2SLS-the study finds that oil rents have exerted a positive and statistically significant effect on diversification, supporting the "resource blessing" hypothesis. Vision 2030 is associated with a significant upward level shift in the diversification index. FDI, however, remains statistically insignificant across all specifications, suggesting that foreign capital has not yet become a primary driver of structural transformation. These findings underscore the central role of coherent stateled policy in navigating the transition beyond hydrocarbon dependence.

title: The Adoption of Digital Payment Effect on Small Vendor Profitability
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: The Adoption of Digital Payment Effect on Small Vendor Profitability
detail.abstract: Micro, small, and medium-sized enterprises (MSMEs) form the backbone of Uzbekistan's economy, constituting an estimated 85 percent of all business establishments, employing nearly 80 percent of the non-agricultural labor force, and contributing 53 percent to GDP and 25 percent to exports (Central Bank of Uzbekistan, 2025). Despite their economic significance, access to formal financial services remains a critical challenge, with fewer than 10 percent of MSMEs having access to bank financing. As of October 2025, over 1.21 million active small business entities operate in the country, including 479,000 small enterprises and microfirms, and 281,900 individual entrepreneurs, yet only 48 percent currently utilize digital payment systems. This study investigates the impact of transitioning from cash-based transactions to digital payment platforms-specifically Click, Uzum, Humo, Uzcard, e-wallets, Google Pay, Apple Pay, and NFC (Near Field Communication) technology-on the profitability and operational efficiency of small vendors in Uzbekistan. Employing a mixed-method approach, the research combines a comprehensive review of existing academic literature with an original survey conducted among small vendors across the country. Data were collected and analyzed regarding transaction costs, payment processing speed, security perceptions, and overall profit margins. The findings reveal that well-integrated digital systems, particularly e-wallets and NFCbased contactless payments, possess significant potential to reduce transaction fees, accelerate payment processing, and expand access to formal financial services for microentrepreneurs. However, the study also identifies substantial barriers to widespread adoption, including inadequate modern financial infrastructure in rural areas, persistent security concerns, and anxieties related to tax compliance. The research concludes that while digital payment systems offer measurable benefits for financial inclusion and operational efficiency among Uzbek microentrepreneurs, their full potential remains constrained by infrastructural and regulatory gaps. Policy interventions aimed at improving digital literacy, strengthening cybersecurity measures, and expanding rural payment infrastructure are essential to maximizing the positive impact of this ongoing financial transition.

detail.abstract: Despite decades of policy interventions and socioeconomic progress, substantial gender disparities remain deeply entrenched in the United States labor market. This paper examines these persistent outcomes with a focus on prime-age workers (ages 25-54) between 2014 and 2024, a demographic selected to ensure data consistency while minimizing confounding education or retirement factors. Utilizing empirical data from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) and the Current Population Survey (CPS), the analysis evaluates structural employment rates, occupational segregation, the gender wage gap, and hiring discrimination. The findings reveal a stagnant 10-percentage-point gap in employment rates favoring men since 2014 and an enduring wage gap where women's median earnings stood at 81.6% of men's in 2018. We argue 1 that the disproportionate burden of childcare and domestic responsibilities serves as the primary mechanism driving these inequities, fundamentally constraining female labor supply and shifting women into flexible but lower-paying roles. Furthermore, traditional labor surveys obscure these nuances by relying on crude occupation codes that fail to differentiate between rigid "greedy jobs" dominated by men and more flexible, lower-compensated positions. The paper concludes by presenting targeted policy interventions, emphasizing that closing the aggregate gender gap requires subsidized universal childcare, expanded parental leave, pay transparency, and a structural shift away from rigid work hour models.

title: Lack of Trust and Fiscal Dominance: Evidence from a Firm Survey Experiment

detail.title: Lack of Trust and Fiscal Dominance: Evidence from a Firm Survey Experiment
detail.abstract:
We study how debt news shapes firms’ inflation expectations in a monetary union. In an active-control experiment, German firms receive optimistic or pessimistic projections of France, Italy, and Spain’s debt-to-GDP ratios. Pessimistic news raises debt beliefs and increases one- and three-year inflation expectations, with no detectable effect at five years. The response is driven by low-trust firms and by firms expecting relatively low ECB policy rates. A salient German debt-financed fiscal shock generates no comparable response. Within a Fisherian framework, the evidence suggests that debt news becomes inflationary when firms perceive incomplete fiscal backing and expect monetary accommodation.

title: The Value of One Office Day a Month

detail.title: The Value of One Office Day a Month
detail.abstract:
Remote work has expanded rapidly, but the value of regular in-person contact remains unclear. We report a randomized controlled trial in which a large multinational randomly assigned 248 customer-service employees to remain fully remote or to work at the office together one day a month. Monthly office days gradually increased productivity, with treated employees handling 7.8% more calls per hour in the post-intervention period. Office days also strengthened workplace communication: treated employees spent 36 additional minutes communicating with colleagues in the week after an office visit, were more likely to report receiving manager feedback, and employee pairs randomly assigned as desk neighbors were 11 percentage points more likely to communicate afterward. In addition, monthly office days reduced attrition by a third. The resulting gains in productivity and retention generated a benefit–cost ratio of about 5:1. These findings show that limited, coordinated in-person contact can improve communication, performance, and retention in remote teams.

detail.abstract: Large language models produce linguistically coherent output without intention, without epistemic access to truth, and without a will of their own. They are not subjects of law. They are instrumenta vocalia — speaking instruments — in the sense Roman law defined two millennia ago: tools that speak without thereby acquiring subjectivity. This paper advances a single thesis. The doctrine of instrumentum vocale cum voluntate domini inscripta, the speaking instrument with the will of the master inscribed, applies only where revocability and evolution under the master are both present. If either condition fails, the doctrine does not partially degrade; it ceases to apply. From this thesis, the paper derives four boundaries that mark the foundation on which any institutional response to AI-mediated decision chains must build. The boundaries are not architectural specifications; they identify the conditions under which records can be reliable, verification can speak from a defensible position, verification can graduate with the territory, and human decisions can be real. The first three boundaries are mathematical: Goedel and Turing (self-attestation), Tarski (truth predicate), Popper (falsifiability), with Austin (speech acts) sharpening the condition for the speaking instrument. The fourth boundary is a convergence of three registers: philosophical (Kant, Schopenhauer), mathematical (Von Foerster, second-order cybernetics), and legal (Habermas, non-delegable duty). The paper traces the global domain movement across seventeen jurisdictions in nine languages, on two doctrinal axes: the verification-failure axis culminating in three high-authority judicial decisions across three legal systems in early 2026, and the privilege and discovery axis defining the procedural conditions under which AI may be used at all, and locates the architecture as the operational implementation of a norm courts and institutions have already begun to recognise. The contribution traces the arc from liability (post-hoc allocation of responsibility through legal proceedings) to embedded accountability (continuous recording of responsibility through architectural substrate), argues that the two are not alternatives but layers, and closes by naming the institutional questions the doctrine opens (regulatory, contractual, professional, international) without prescribing a single resolution among them.

title: Bank Resources, Structured Bond Withdrawal, and Securities Subsidiary Profitability: Evidence from Regional Banking Groups in Japan

detail.title: Bank Resources, Structured Bond Withdrawal, and Securities Subsidiary Profitability: Evidence from Regional Banking Groups in Japan
detail.abstract: This study examines whether parent or sister bank resources are associated with the profitability of securities subsidiaries and whether subsidiary profitability declined during the period of intensified withdrawal from structured bond intermediation and sales from fiscal year 2022 onward. Using 127 firm-year observations of securities subsidiaries affiliated with Japanese regional banking groups from fiscal years 2018–2024, this study analyzes return on assets, return on equity, and the trading income ratio. The results show that parent or sister bank resources, proxied by the number of employees, branch networks, and total assets, are not positively associated with subsidiary profitability. In contrast, subsidiary profitability, particularly the trading income ratio, declined significantly from fiscal year 2022 onward. These results are consistent with the view that securities subsidiaries may have relied heavily on high-margin structured bonds and that supervisory tightening may constrain the profitability of product-dependent business models within regional banking groups. This study contributes to the literature on financial institutions by providing subsidiary-level evidence on the relationship between banking group resources, product-market regulatory changes, and the profitability of nontraditional financial activities.

title: The Strategic Choice of Spatial Price Policy: Mixed Strategies Challenge the Classic Prisoner's Dilemma

detail.title: The Strategic Choice of Spatial Price Policy: Mixed Strategies Challenge the Classic Prisoner's Dilemma
detail.abstract: In a seminal contribution, Thisse and Vives (1988) demonstrate that, in a two-stage pricing policy/price game, price discrimination emerges as a dominant strategy, trapping firms into a Prisoner's Dilemma, both in a linear city model with linear transport costs and in a circular market model with quadratic transport costs. Their result has profoundly shaped subsequent research in economics, management, and finance. Importantly, they make a specific modelling choice. Because the asymmetric subgames admit no pure-strategy Nash equilibrium under simultaneous price competition, they adopt the sequential Stackelberg standard: the mill-pricing firm becomes the price leader and the discriminatory firm responds optimally. Here, rather than modifying the original framework, I compute the unique mixed-strategy Nash equilibrium for asymmetric subgames. The main finding overturns the standard conclusion under maximum differentiation: the Prisoner's Dilemma vanishes, and the pricing-policy game becomes a coordination game, where mutual uniform pricing Pareto dominates mutual discrimination. In the linear-city framework, however, sufficiently large marginal-cost asymmetries restore price discrimination as a dominant strategy, so that the pricingpolicy game mayor may not-exhibit the structure of a Prisoner's Dilemma.

detail.abstract: The Generalized Autoregressive Conditional Heteroskedasticity (GARCH) framework introduced by Bollerslev remains one of the standard tools for modeling conditional volatility in financial time series, value-at-risk measurement, and related applications. At the same time, recent literature shows that the contemporary development of GARCH-based research has been shaped by several recurring themes, including asymmetric volatility modeling, dynamic dependence structures, estimation under heavy tails, and hybrid forecasting architectures. This review provides a selective narrative survey of recent developments while restricting detailed discussion to studies whose bibliographic information can be checked or substantially corroborated. In addition to recent work, the paper includes an earlier Chinese-language contribution by Yang (2012) as a background reference for distributional assumptions in VaRoriented GARCH applications.

title: Portfolio Complexity and Its Impact on Risk-Adjusted Returns and Volatility: Evidence from Equity Portfolios

detail.title: Portfolio Complexity and Its Impact on Risk-Adjusted Returns and Volatility: Evidence from Equity Portfolios
detail.abstract: This study investigates the impact of portfolio complexity on volatility and risk-adjusted returns in equity portfolios. While diversification is widely recognized as a method for reducing unsystematic risk, the optimal level of portfolio complexity remains a subject of debate. The research examines whether increasing the number of holdings continuously improves portfolio performance or whether excessive diversification introduces estimation challenges that reduce efficiency. Using secondary market data, multiple equally weighted portfolios of varying sizes were constructed and evaluated through volatility and Sharpe ratio analysis. The findings indicate that portfolio expansion initially produces substantial diversification benefits by reducing volatility and improving risk-adjusted performance. However, once portfolio size exceeds the optimal range of approximately 10-15 holdings, the incremental benefits of diversification begin to decline while the estimation burden associated with a larger number of assets increases. The results suggest that portfolios containing a moderate number of holdings achieve a more favorable balance between diversification efficiency and estimation stability than highly concentrated or excessively diversified portfolios. The study contributes to the portfolio management literature by providing empirical evidence that portfolio complexity exhibits diminishing marginal benefits and that optimal portfolio construction requires balancing risk reduction with estimation considerations. These findings offer practical insights for investors and portfolio managers seeking to improve portfolio efficiency under realistic market conditions.

title: Objective Approach to Comparative Business Valuation: Market Multiples, Country Risk, and Machine Learning Techniques

detail.title: Objective Approach to Comparative Business Valuation: Market Multiples, Country Risk, and Machine Learning Techniques
detail.abstract: This paper introduces an objective, globally scalable algorithm designed as a practical tool for estimating the probable market capitalization of any sufficiently large and profitable company operating within a country with a sovereign credit rating. The model incorporates country-risk adjustments, industry-level stratification, and Ridge-regression-based predictions using five observable financial metrics: Book Value, Sales, Operating Income, Earnings, and Debt. Empirical testing on 1,240 U.S.-listed companies demonstrates an accuracy acceptable for valuation practice. Implemented as a ready-to-use calculator the method establishes a benchmark for company value within the market valuation approach, simulating public stock-market trading conditions. It serves as a unified, worldwide measurement tool for business valuation, relying explicitly on observable market data and financial reports while remaining free of any subjective assumptions. Accordingly, this approach is applicable for reporting the fair value of investments in compliance with International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS). The resulting benchmark reflects minority interest value and requires subsequent adjustments for control, lack of marketability, and other company-specific factors which are not captured by the algorithm but essential for business valuation practice.

title:
Optimal Control in Unsecured Credit: 
The Asymmetric "Bang-Bang" Effect in the U.S. Credit Card Market

detail.title:
Optimal Control in Unsecured Credit: 
The Asymmetric "Bang-Bang" Effect in the U.S. Credit Card Market
detail.abstract: This paper develops and tests an empirically tractable model of optimal credit-supply policy in the U.S. credit card market. Three contributions distinguish the analysis from the existing literature. First, we cast the bank's discretionary tightening decision as a continuous-time Hamiltonian control problem in which the shadow price of credit-the marginal contribution of a unit of new origination to franchise value-is the endogenous object the bank manages. Second, we exploit the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau's (CFPB) micro-aggregated dataset, which disaggregates monthly credit card origination into five FICO risk tiers (Deep Subprime, Subprime, Near Prime, Prime, Super-prime). Treating these tiers as the panel dimension yields 1,105 tier-month observations from January 2007 to July 2025, an order of magnitude more statistical power than aggregate quarterly samples, while preserving genuine borrower heterogeneity. Third, we test the central prediction of the bang-bang Pontryagin solution-that supply tightening should be discrete and concentrated on high-risk exposures-using a stratified panel-FE specification with a tierinteracted control term. Across multiple identifications (single-equation OLS, SVAR with Cholesky ordering, Random Forest forecast of the tightening regime, and Mincer-Zarnowitz evaluation), the absolute response of subprime origination to a one-unit tightening shock is roughly twice that of super-prime origination (β =-0.020 vs.-0.009; interaction p < 0.005). The findings hold up under cross-validation against the Federal Reserve's quarterly bank-level charge-off and delinquency series. The framework provides a forward-looking, regulator-friendly diagnostic that complements the scenario-based logic of CECL, IFRS 9, and the Basel IV output floor.

title: Assessing the Impact of Domestic Credit on Economic Performance in Ghana: An Instrumental Variable Model

detail.title: Assessing the Impact of Domestic Credit on Economic Performance in Ghana: An Instrumental Variable Model
detail.abstract: Domestic credit growth has remained a central policy concern in Africa, where financial deepening is often accompanied by structural inefficiencies that limit its contribution to sustainable development. In Ghana, despite persistent credit expansion, questions remain as to whether this growth fuels productive investment or merely supports consumption and fiscal imbalances. This study examines the impact of domestic credit on economic performance in Ghana, engaging the debate on whether credit expansion serves as an enabler of growth or a constraint. The precise effect of credit on real GDP per capita remains ambiguous, partly due to endogeneity and reverse causality. Using a Two-Stage Least Squares (2SLS) instrumental variable approach over the 1984-2023 period, the analysis employs broad money supply as an instrument for domestic credit while controlling for gross capital formation, government expenditure, inflation, and trade openness. The findings reveal a significant bidirectional relationship between credit and growth, indicating that credit expansion alone does not guarantee sustained performance without addressing inefficiencies in allocation. The results further show that government expenditure and trade openness enhance growth, while inflation has a negative effect. This study concludes that financial sector reforms, improved credit targeting, prudent fiscal management, and strengthened trade competitiveness are critical for maximising the developmental impact of domestic credit in Ghana.

detail.abstract:
We study a specific but important failure mode in financial LLMs: numerical 
errors in task-specifically fine-tuned small models are statistically 
structured rather than random (chi-squared = 41.97, p < 0.001), and this 
structure makes deterministic post-hoc correction more effective than 
reasoning augmentation in our controlled experiments. Scaling reasoning via 
chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) — 
the dominant paradigms for improving LLM numerical accuracy — both degrade 
performance in this setting (CoT: -9.0pp; RAG: -7.5pp; p < 0.001, 
McNemar's test).

We propose a Deterministic Verification Layer (DVL) — a parameter-free, 
inference-time module that exploits this structured error distribution to 
improve execution accuracy from 1.0% to 42.61% (95% CI: 39.5–45.7%) on 
FinQA through document context and QLoRA fine-tuning. DVL logs 63 
corrections across three rule types with 100% correction precision on the 
audited subset (44/44 verified correct, zero false positives). All three 
rules fire on prediction magnitude, question keywords, and document-context 
unit headers — no ground-truth access at inference. DVL generalizes across 
architectures (Llama-3-8B: +10.31pp without retraining), across financial 
benchmarks (TAT-QA zero-shot: +9.47pp and +19.92pp; p < 0.001, McNemar 
c = 0), and captures 45.8% of gains achievable by full symbolic 
recomputation (93.13% oracle accuracy) without gold program annotations. 
A cross-domain evaluation on DROP establishes that the structured bias is 
specific to financial training distributions, not a universal LLM property. 
A mechanistic analysis identifies computational drift as the CoT failure 
mode: output length increases 17x with zero extraction failures, and a 
token-level trace shows arithmetic precision degrading at step boundaries. 
Our system narrows the gap to GPT-3.5 (no CoT) to 5.4pp using a model 25x 
smaller, on a single consumer GPU, with deterministic auditable outputs.

title: Interconnected, Self-Organizing, and Forgetting: A Unified Theory of Economic Canopy Dynamics Working Paper -2025

detail.title: Interconnected, Self-Organizing, and Forgetting: A Unified Theory of Economic Canopy Dynamics Working Paper -2025
detail.abstract: Two earlier working papers by the present author-one describing the structure and equilibrium of a generalized economic canopy (Amavilah, 2005), the other modeling the Ebbinghaus forgetting effect on net learning in production systems (Amavilah, 2003)-are here integrated with the theory of self-organized criticality (SOC; Bak, Tang, and Wiesenfeld, 1987, 1988) and the knowledge-dynamics framework of Hidalgo (2025). The synthesis yields a unified model in which economies are simultaneously interconnected (epiphytic, parasitic, and host relationships), self-organizing toward a critical threshold, and subject to decay of accumulated knowledge and capability. Growth, stagnation, and decline are all endogenous outcomes; the capacity of any economy to grow depends not only on its own performance trajectory but on whether the knowledge embedded in its canopy relationships is being retained, forgotten, or replenished. We derive modified Lotka-Volterra competition equations augmented with Ebbinghaus-type forgetting operators and SOC avalanche dynamics, propose five empirically testable propositions, and outline a panel data strategy for implementation.

detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence has revived fundamental questions concerning human dignity, moral agency, economic organization, and the future of human flourishing. This paper examines these questions through insights drawn from Pope Francis (Laudato Si', 2015; Fratelli Tutti, 2020) and Pope Leo XIV (Magnifica Humanitas, 2026), arguing that contemporary debates about artificial intelligence ultimately depend upon deeper, largely unexamined assumptions regarding the human person, social welfare, and the common good. The paper makes three contributions. First, it develops a formal critique of conventional welfare economics by introducing a multi-dimensional welfare functional W(U, S, D, E, C, L) that supplements utility U with solidarity S, dignity D, ecological integrity E, community cohesion C, and moral agency L. Second, it formally distinguishes human intelligence HI = (C, E, M, R, T) from artificial intelligence AI = g(D data , A, Θ), characterizing the irreducibility of conscious, embodied, relational cognition. Third, it introduces a welfare dynamics model in which AI enters as a vector of four channelsproductivity p, displacement q, surveillance r, and autonomy erosion sand derives a dignity constraint that bounds economically optimal deployment of AI systems. The paper further introduces an AI concentration index to capture power asymmetries in the governance of large-scale AI systems, and integrates these elements into a holistic model of the human person. A central finding is that AI may increase aggregate output while simultaneously reducing welfare if dignity, community cohesion, and moral agency deteriorate, even under conditions of Pareto-efficient allocation. This result extends the Sen (1979) critique of Paretian welfarism to the technological domain, and provides formal grounding for the pastoral concerns articulated in papal social thought.

detail.title: Optimal Structure of Penalties with Judgment-Proof Injurers

publicationDetails.journalName: CEIS: Centre for Economic & International Studies Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: I characterize the optimal regulation of a firm constituted by potential judgment-proof agents. I investigate two cases: (i) A principal hires an agent to undertake a prevention effort on their behalf; (ii) Two agents are jointly responsible of undertaking a prevention effort. In both cases, agents are in charge of exerting an unobservable level of safety care to reduce the probability of an accident that may occur due to the firm risky activity. Agents are called judgment proof when their final wealth is not enough to pay for the monetary penalties imposed by the regulator. I show that the standard Equivalence Theorem, stating that the distribution of penalties among injurers is irrelevant, does not hold in this context. Instead, in a principal-agent firm, the optimal regulation requires to fully target the principal if the agent can be subject to judgment proofness. In a two-agent firm, the optimal regulation consists in an almost equal sharing of penalties among agents.
