detail.abstract:
This paper develops a variational decision architecture grounded in the minimisation of Expected Free Energy
(EFE). Behaviour is modelled as the selection of policies that preserve consistency between anticipated
outcomes, preference priors, epistemic value, temporal scope, and identity stability within a single Bayesian
generative architecture. Rationality is thereby reframed as variational coherence (internal consistency of
prediction and preference) rather than expected-utility maximisation.
Within this framework, classical Expected Utility theory emerges as a mathematically exact limiting regime
under explicitly stated embedding conditions (including entropy neutrality over the relevant comparison set,
zero epistemic weighting, and zero complexity cost), while entropy heterogeneity, epistemic valuation,
temporal precision, and complexity rigidity generate systematic decision structure that cannot, in general, be
represented by a scalar expected-utility functional.
In this paper, we formally
(A) derive the conditions under which Expected Free Energy collapses to Expected Utility;
(B) show that Prospect-Theory-like asymmetries, Rational Inattention–type information regularisation, and
identity-preserving rigidity arise as internal regimes of a single objective instead of behavioural add-ons;
and
(C) demonstrate that decision regimes correspond to attractors in an Expected Free Energy landscape whose
geometry supports stability, hysteresis, and bifurcations.
Numerical analyses (illustrative simulations in explicitly defined task environments) show that persistence,
abrupt regime change, and path dependence arise lawfully from parameterised precision structure without
post-hoc behavioural assumptions.
Finally, we provide an implementation-level audit of empirical discipline. The framework’s hyperparameters
have distinct behavioural signatures and are locally structurally identifiable in principle under pre-specified
separability conditions, and cross-fitting diagnostics show that, in controlled data-generating processes with
held-out evaluation, the full EFE architecture is rejectable out of sample when its additional structure is absent,
while remaining discriminable from nested restrictions and a matched Rational Inattention alternative.
The result is a compact, mathematically explicit, and empirically testable decision architecture, whereby
Expected Free Energy does not replace classical theories, but locates them. It specifies where they are valid,
where they fail, and why. By doing so, Expected Free Energy provides a structural, falsifiable foundation for
cumulative work on choice.

detail.abstract: Financial institutions face greater regulatory obligations than almost any other type of organization. Since 2009, fines and settlements paid by major banks have increased by nearly 45 times relative to operating income (Kaminski and Robu, 2016), yet most institutions continue to rely on manual compliance procedures that are slow, inconsistent, and reactive. This paper examines whether formal methods-mathematical techniques for specifying and verifying the behavior of business processes-can provide a more systematic and auditable basis for compliance in banks, insurers, and asset managers. Drawing on nine papers from the academic literature, including a systematic review of 46 primary studies spanning three decades (López and Hildebrandt, 2024), it distinguishes carefully between what the literature proves, what it suggests but does not prove, and what the authors propose as a practical synthesis for financial institutions. The central finding is that no single formalism is sufficient. Model checking is the most proven technique for design-time process verification but handles run-time monitoring and normative richness poorly. Deontic logic correctly captures obligations, permissions, and escalation chains but lacks mature tooling (Governatori and Rotolo, 2010). Pattern-based compliance languages, developed in collaboration with major professional services firms, offer the most promising path to making formal verification accessible to compliance officers (Elgammal et al., 2016). Most tools remain at prototype stage. The paper proposes a layered architecture combining readable process models for business users, pattern-based compliance rules for compliance officers, formal verification for process designers, and operational rule monitoring for audit evidence. This is the author's practical synthesis rather than a conclusion the literature establishes directly. Formal methods cannot replace professional legal judgment, and the translation of regulatory text into formal rules remains the principal adoption barrier.

title: Authorship in the Age of Machines: AI-Generated Works, Legal Personhood, and the Case for Copyright Reform in Nepal

detail.title: Authorship in the Age of Machines: AI-Generated Works, Legal Personhood, and the Case for Copyright Reform in Nepal
detail.abstract: Who authors a poem composed by a large language model? Who owns an image generated by a diffusion system trained on millions of copyrighted photographs? These questions, once confined to academic speculation, have become pressing legal and commercial concerns as generative artificial intelligence becomes embedded in creative industries worldwide. This article examines the authorship and ownership dimensions of AI-generated works through the lens of Nepali copyright law, arguing that the anthropocentric framework embedded in Section 2(a) of the Copyright Act, 2059 (2002) renders Nepal wholly unprepared to address the creative and economic realities of the AI era. Drawing on comparative analysis of the United Kingdom's surrogate authorship model, the United States' human-authorship requirement, and the evolving international debate within WIPO, the article contends that Nepal must pursue three interconnected reforms: the introduction of a conditional surrogate authorship mechanism for computer-generated works; the clarification of ownership rights in human-AI collaborative outputs; and the development of a moral rights framework adequate to protect the dignity and economic interests of human creators in an environment of automated creative production. The article situates these proposals within Nepal's constitutional framework and its obligations under the Berne Convention and TRIPS, and argues that reform in this area is not merely a technical legal necessity but a matter of constitutional and developmental significance.

detail.abstract:
Background: Supporting working-age patients with cancer requires understanding factors affecting employment retention. We investigated gender disparities and underlying mechanisms in employment continuity following colorectal cancer (CRC) surgery.

Methods: This nationwide retrospective cohort study used the Japan Health Insurance Association (JHIA) database. Participants were insured individuals aged 15–56 years who underwent surgery within 4 months of their first CRC claim (April 2016–March 2020). Withdrawals during the 3-year follow-up were classified into death or resignation. Gender differences were analysed using cumulative incidence functions (CIFs) and Fine–Gray models, with death as a competing risk, to estimate subdistribution hazard ratios (SHRs) adjusted for age, company size, and income. Mediation and E-value sensitivity analyses were performed.

Findings: Among 7213 workers (2294 women), the 3-year CIF for resignation was higher in women (24·7% vs. 19·0%), while death was higher in men (6·4% vs. 4·1%). The absolute gender difference in resignation widened up to 12 months post-surgery, then levelled off. In Fine–Gray models, after adjusting for income, women’s higher resignation risk was no longer statistically significant. Conversely, lower income, younger age, and larger company size (observed uniquely among women) independently predicted higher resignation risk. Mediation analysis revealed that income explained 84·9% of the gender difference. Sensitivity analysis using E-values confirmed result robustness.

Interpretation: Gender disparities in job resignation following CRC surgery are driven by baseline income inequalities. Achieving gender equity for cancer survivors requires interventions targeting economically vulnerable workers within 12 months of diagnosis, alongside efforts to mitigate structural income inequality in Japan.

title: Taxing the Theft of Africa's Small Pelagic Fisheries
affiliations: Pepperdine University

detail.title: Taxing the Theft of Africa's Small Pelagic Fisheries
detail.abstract: Recent decades have seen an escalation of trawlers illegally targeting small pelagic stocks in shallow waters and passing them off as by-catch to avoid tax in many coastal African countries. This paper analyzes the crowding and ecosystem externalities that ensue from these illegal fishing activities and proposes an optimal tax strategy using a two-sector bioeconomic model. The theoretical model is empirically estimated using multiple steps of regression analysis and data from Ghana from 1986 to 2013. Beginning with a reduced major axis regression between catch and fishing effort, the paper estimates stock abundance within the small pelagic zone at 1,990,337,382 metric tons. The stock transition equation and the equation governing the evolution of effort within the open access artisanal fishery model were also empirically estimated using ordinary least squares regression and controlling for ecological factors like salinity, upwelling, and local temperature. The parameter estimates from the multiple regressions were used to calibrate the optimal tax rate to be approximately 40.4%. At a 40.4% tax rate, by-catch fell by about 40.3%. While data challenges may bias the estimates downward, the most significant finding here is that there is a near proportional relationship between the tax rate and by-catch reduction. The study recommends that the government should increase taxes on by-catch by at least 40%, and improve inshore monitoring and reporting of harvests of both targeted stocks and by-catch in order to reduce illegal targeting of small pelagic stocks.

title: People, Power, Process: Heuristic design principles for democratic planning
affiliations: University College London, University of Lausanne, University of Lausanne and University of Leeds - Sustainability Research Institute

detail.title: People, Power, Process: Heuristic design principles for democratic planning
detail.abstract: Democratic planning scholarship proposes to reverse neoliberal market fundamentalism. However, proposals often graft radical direct decision-making onto liberal democratic frameworks, creating a tension that limits transformative potential. This paper presents a critical theoretical investigation which can act as a foundation for democratic planning towards a radical political potential, beyond institutional design. First, we analyse the liberal theory of constituent power, tracing its evolution from revolutionary justification to the contemporary pacification within constitutional orders which separate the economic from the political, thereby safeguarding capitalism from democratic contestation. Second, we build on Gramscian hegemony and Foucauldian governmentality to reveal the cultural-ideological and subject-forming mechanisms that naturalise market logics and suppress collective desire. Finally, we engage Deleuze and Guattari’ s ontology of desire as an affirmative, collective force and their concepts of deterritorialisation, reterritorialisation and lines of flight to envisage an escape from the constraints of liberalism and hegemonic control. Synthesising this analysis, we suggest three design principles for a radical planning praxis: (1) dynamic stability, promoting fluid institutional design, (2) design for criticism, destruction and escape, building institutions that invite their own contestation; and (3) active subject formation, crafting material and affective conditions to catalyse democratic assemblages. We conclude that by confronting these deeper political problematics democratic planning might be able to overcome liberalism’s constitutive limits and forge genuine collective power.

detail.abstract:
An alegal—or, put another way, lawless—methodology is quite commonplace in U.S. antitrust decision-making and discourse.  For decades, antitrust viewed itself as “exceptional” and “peculiar” in this regard.  The conventional excuse, first offered by scholars associated with the Chicago School, is that the antitrust statutes are so vague as to be content-free, a “blank check” for judges.  But as recent academic research makes clear, that notion cannot withstand scrutiny even as to the Sherman Act, let alone the Clayton Act or Federal Trade Commission Act.  That said, existing critiques of antitrust’s alegal turn have not yet exposed its sheer breadth and depth.  

This Essay examines lawless antitrust in action.  It excavates a swath of alegal moves that occurred during the “End of Antitrust History” period stretching from roughly 1980 through 2020.  Fully appreciating the breadth and depth of lawless antitrust is essential for understanding a fundamental—yet underappreciated and often misunderstood—pillar of the new antimonopoly school.  Their revival of law—paying attention to statutory text, understanding legislative purposes and structures, and following applicable precedent—was not blind formalism.  Nor was it the product of naïve nostalgia for a bygone era.  Methodology matters.  Without a role for law, there can be no rule of law.  It follows that rejecting lawless antitrust is essential if we are to have a healthy antitrust enterprise.

title: Speed Does Not Increase Job Displacement: A Bottleneck Theorem for AI Speedup and Labor
affiliations: and Liminal Capital

detail.title: Speed Does Not Increase Job Displacement: A Bottleneck Theorem for AI Speedup and Labor
detail.abstract: Does faster AI displace more workers? We prove that it does not, once "faster" is defined precisely. We distinguish speed (performing the AI's existing tasks more quickly, at fixed quality) from rising adoption of automation and gains in capability, the true sources of displacement. The proof is a bottleneck result. A completed unit of work has a part that AI can perform and a complementary part that requires a human, so output is set by whichever side is slower. Speed raises the capacity of the AI side only. When the AI side is slower, faster AI raises output. When the human step is slower, output is capped and faster AI merely produces idle capacity. Speed therefore has no displacement margin of its own, and the displacement specification of Verschuere and Cameron (2026a) correctly carries no speed term: substitutable work is captured by adoption, and complementary work is invariant to speed.

title: Regime-Preserving Bootstrap for FX Fair-Value Models

detail.title: Regime-Preserving Bootstrap for FX Fair-Value Models
detail.abstract:
This paper documents a regime-preserving bootstrap procedure for validating the out-of sample robustness of FX fair-value strategies (BEER, FEER, PPP). The central idea is that standard bootstrap methods (IID, Moving Block, Stationary Block) destroy the economic regime structure of macro-FX data and thereby systematically bias Sharpe ratio inference. We propose two regime-aware resamplers-Regime-Uniform (block resampling within macroregimes) and Regime-Markov (block resampling with calibrated Markov transition matrix)and validate them using five structure metrics, a Sharpe loss metric, an arrangement distance, a stationarity gate per Section 11.7, and Wilcoxon paired tests with Benjamini-Hochberg FDR.

Applied to a BEER pricer for three currency pairs (EURUSD, GBPUSD, USDJPY) with B = 1999 bootstrap replicates, the key finding is: Regime-Markov reduces the bootstrap Sharpe loss by a factor of 1.3× compared to Regime-Uniform (the simpler block resampler without transition structure) and by a factor of 4.6× compared to the naive IID benchmark. The Markov transition structure provides the additional gain over pure block resampling. The calibrated transition matrix passes the Section 11.7 stationarity gate (TV drift = 0.10), validating forward projections over short horizons of ∼3-5 Markov steps. We document the complete metric definitions, the implementation, and the honest limits of cross-pair generalization.

detail.abstract:
Background: Child stunting remains a major public health challenge in Ecuador, particularly in vulnerable territories. Evidence on how household-level territorial determinants influence stunting across contrasting contexts is limited. This study analyzed determinants associated with stunting in Santa Elena (coastal) and Colta (Andean), two territories with a high burden of child malnutrition.

Methods: This cross-sectional study used household survey data collected between April and December 2025 from 605 households with 653 children aged 0–59 months. Stunting was defined as height-for-age Z-scores below −2 SD (WHO standards). Separate logistic regression models were estimated for each municipality, incorporating socioeconomic, housing (including WASH), food security, healthcare access, and caregiver knowledge variables. Results were reported as odds ratios and marginal effects.

Findings: Determinants differed substantially between municipalities. In Colta, environmental conditions and caregiver knowledge were most influential. Overcrowding doubled stunting risk (OR=2.06; p=0.013), while higher knowledge reduced it (OR=0.07; p=0.037). WASH deficiencies significantly increased stunting, especially in rural communities. In Santa Elena, socioeconomic status was the primary determinant, with children in the lowest wealth quintile facing four times higher risk (OR=4.21; p=0.007). Environmental risks and age (>2 years) were also significant, while WASH deficiencies showed a counterintuitive association with stunting.

Interpretation: Stunting determinants are strongly shaped by territorial context. Behavioral and environmental factors dominate in Colta, while socioeconomic inequalities are central in Santa Elena. These findings support territorially tailored strategies combining structural and behavioral interventions, including both prevention and post-1,000 days nutritional recovery.

detail.abstract:
This paper introduces the Village Productivity Index (VPI), also designated by its Indonesian term Indeks Produktivitas Desa (IPD), as a novel composite framework for measuring the economic productivity of Indonesian villages as productive territorial units. Existing village assessment instruments in Indonesia, including the Village Development Index (IDM), SDGs Desa, and the Indeks Desa framework, primarily focus on administrative performance, service delivery, and institutional compliance, while providing limited measurement of actual economic value creation. This paper conceptualizes this gap as a Productivity Measurement Deficit in Indonesian village governance.

Drawing upon institutional economics, productivity theory, development economics, and the OECD New Rural Paradigm, the paper argues for a paradigm shift from the “administrative village” model toward the “productive village” model. The proposed VPI framework consists of five dimensions: Agricultural and Primary Sector Productivity, Local Economic Diversification, Labor Productivity and Human Capital Utilization, Village Fiscal Efficiency and Economic Return on Dana Desa, and Market Linkage and Economic Integration.

Methodologically, the framework employs Winsorized normalization at the 5th and 95th percentiles to reduce outlier distortion and incorporates a three-year moving average to estimate the economic return of village fiscal transfers. Simulation exercises involving representative village archetypes demonstrate the index’s diagnostic and discriminatory capacity. Comparative analysis shows that the VPI complements existing frameworks by directly measuring economic productivity rather than administrative or social performance.

The paper concludes with policy recommendations for integrating VPI into Dana Desa allocation mechanisms, performance-based fiscal incentives, and national rural development planning. As a conceptual working paper, the framework provides a foundation for future empirical validation and contributes to broader debates on rural productivity, decentralization, and evidence-based village development policy.

detail.abstract: This letter examines stock-price reactions to three public generative AI events at a comparable product stage: the release of Google Gemini 3 (18 November 2025), the launch of Google Project Genie (29 January 2026), and the public availability of the Claude legal/Cowork plug-in, mapped to the 30 January 2026 trading session. The analysis applies a market model to Alphabet as the originator, to the gaming portfolio, and to the professional-information portfolio, with a consumer-staples portfolio as a low-directexposure negative control, and follows prices through one trading quarter ([0,+63]). After Gemini 3, Alphabet's cumulative abnormal return in [0,+5] was +10.77% (t = +2.72), rising to +13.09% (t = +3.26) against the technology benchmark XLK. After Project Genie, the gaming portfolio's average cumulative abnormal return was-13.00% (t =-4.67) and remained negative after one quarter (-14.40%). After Claude, the comparable return for the professional-information portfolio was-14.67% (t =-6.95) in [0,+5] and reversed to +7.77% after one quarter. Treated-minus-control differences in [0,+5] were-22.06 pp for gaming and-23.74 pp for professional information. For Claude, the analysis also applies a conditional reverse DCF that maps implied revenue-erosion paths (0.68-1.92 pp per year in the no-marginbenefit scenario) and audits public disclosures. The letter develops the Asymmetric Intelligence Discount (AID) framework around three dimensions of asymmetry in market attention and formulates three falsifiable directional predictions. The findings document parallel domain repricings and provide an auditable starting point for further tests of the interpretive AID hypothesis.

title: Federal Reserve Communication, Cross-Asset Spillovers, and the Indian Macro Nexus: DCC-GARCH and FinBERT Evidence from the Hiking Cycle (2018-2026)

detail.title: Federal Reserve Communication, Cross-Asset Spillovers, and the Indian Macro Nexus: DCC-GARCH and FinBERT Evidence from the Hiking Cycle (2018-2026)
detail.abstract: We test whether transformer-based sentiment extracted from Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) statements transmits to Indian financial markets over 2018-2026 (n = 2,031 NIFTY trading days, 72 FOMC events). A Federal Hawkishness Index (FHI) is constructed by applying FinBERT-tone (Huang et al., 2023) to each statement and inverting the polarity so that higher values denote more hawkish language. We subject the FHI to a layered econometric framework: a vector autoregression with Granger causality across four channels (NIFTY returns, INR/USD, 10-year G-Sec yields, FII equity flows), a DCC-GARCH model of the NIFTY-S&P 500 conditional correlation, a Chow/Bai-Perron structural-break analysis, a nested incrementalinformation test pitting FHI against the contemporaneous federal-funds-rate change, and a ±δ-threshold backtest net of India transaction costs. The aggregate verdict is panel-dependent. On the full 2018-2026 sample the FHI Granger-causes NIFTY returns (F = 2.247, p = 0.022) and INR/USD changes (F = 2.867, p = 0.006), while under the truncated 2018-2023 sample matching the FII-availability window all four channels fail to reject the null (p ∈ [0.10, 0.90]). The marginal predictive content therefore concentrates in the post-April 2023 segment that the FII cut excludes-the disinflation, cut-cycle preparation, and early Trump 2.0 tariff window. The asymmetry is reinforced by the event-study decomposition: hawkish minus dovish CAR[-1, +1] is-3.366 percentage points during the 2022-2023 hike cycle, a panel-dependent signal, the event-window test localises it to the hike-cycle regime. Economic significance, however, is modest: FHI adds nothing on top of the funds-rate change (Finc = 0.001, p = 0.976), and a sentiment-overlay strategy underperforms buy-and-hold by 10.9 percentage points out of sample. The DCC correlation is significantly time-varying (ˆa+ˆb = 0.514, .ρ = 0.219). Read alongside the alpha-decay finding for domestic sentiment in Maheswari (2026), the picture is one of an emerging market in which exogenous textual signals retain a measurable but regime-localised footprint, even as their directional risk premium is largely competed away once the underlying rate signal is controlled for.

detail.abstract: This document describes the motivation and constrution of the War Index of Hirshleifer, Mai, and Pukthuanthong (2025a), and the War Factor (WarFac) and the war factor-mimicking portfolio (WMP) of Hirshleifer, Mai, and Pukthuanthong (2025b); and describes how to obtain free access to these times series. detail.abstract: Economic liberalization and the removal of capital market restrictions have significantly enhanced global financial integration by facilitating cross-border capital flows and improving resource allocation. Technological progress and financial innovation have further reduced transaction costs and expanded opportunities for international portfolio diversification. In integrated markets, similar assets tend to yield comparable risk-adjusted returns, limiting arbitrage and encouraging investors to diversify across less correlated markets. This study investigates the interrelationships among three major stock markets representing developed and emerging economies: the NASDAQ (United States), the Shanghai Stock Exchange (China), and the National Stock Exchange (India). Employing a Vector Autoregression (VAR) framework and VAR-based Granger causality tests, the research analyses short-run interactions and causal linkages among these markets. The findings contribute to the literature on international stock market integration and offer valuable insights for investors and policymakers regarding diversification strategies and market interdependence in an increasingly globalized financial environment.

title: The Credit Supply Channel of Borrower-Based Measures
affiliations: Banco de España

detail.title: The Credit Supply Channel of Borrower-Based Measures
detail.abstract: This paper studies how borrower-based macroprudential (BBM) policies shape macro-financial dynamics when credit demand and credit supply frictions interact. Using smooth-transition panel local projections for euro-area countries, I show that the macroeconomic effects of adverse credit shocks are significantly larger when household indebtedness and bank fragility are simultaneously elevated. I then show, in a simple theoretical model featuring a collateral constraint and a bank balance-sheet constraint, that this state dependence arises from a feedback loop between collateral values and bank net worth. Quantitative simulations from a medium-scale DSGE model indicate that tighter loan-to-value (LTV) limits dampen downturns not only by restraining leverage ex ante, but also by protecting bank capital and stabilizing credit supply ex post. Welfare comparisons suggest that the benefits of BBM policies increase with housingmarket risk and banking-sector fragility.

title: Towards Trustworthy, Inclusive and Equitable Tourism Carbon Accounting for Just Sustainability Transition: The Tourism Carbon Intelligence System (TCIS) Enabled by Converged AI-Edge-Blockchain Technologies

detail.title: Towards Trustworthy, Inclusive and Equitable Tourism Carbon Accounting for Just Sustainability Transition: The Tourism Carbon Intelligence System (TCIS) Enabled by Converged AI-Edge-Blockchain Technologies
detail.abstract: Tourism indicates a higher carbon intensity compared to other sectors in global economy. Despite the urgency of the Paris Agreement, the tourism industry clearly remains off-track. In our view, the real problems preventing that actions in global tourism carbon governance originates in the structural inadequacies of carbon accounting system. Information, epistemic and distributive gaps make tourism carbon accounting a "black box". Data, methodology and institution deficits are their root causes. To solve these complex gaps results from multifaceted contributing factors, we need a paradigm shift from pure technology to a holistic, systemic restructuring. At first, tourism Carbon Intelligence System (TCIS), a technology framework solution integrating AI, Edge, and Blockchain, lays the technology foundation. The study further bridges the implementation disconnect by proposing three phases of implementation. Considering interest and abilities of different stakeholders in reality and combining theories from social science, TCIS has high possibilities to step forward into real world transition. Through this research work in complete circle, we hope to outline a new pathway for trustworthy, inclusive and equitable tourism carbon accounting for just sustainability transition.

title: "An Important Barrier to 'Doing for Self'"

detail.abstract: This Working Paper continues BlackEconomics.org’s efforts to unscramble the widely held myth that racial discrimination is the primary reason for Black America’s economic and social gaps with non-Black Americans. Concurrence with, and adoption of, racial discrimination as the major cause for these gaps—irrespective of its veracity— is problematic because it minimizes important scholarship; it infers that we do not possess a sound definition of “racial discrimination;” and it engenders space from which to self impose the “soft bigotry of low expectations." Are we our own worst enemy? Do we lack the knowledge, leadership, motivation, confidence, and courage to clarify who and what we are, give credence to that self-knowledge, and then to “do for self?”

title: Platform Liability Avoidance and Indirect Participation: Legal Accountability for Third-Party Uploaded Content and the Limits of Safe Harbor Doctrine

detail.abstract: This paper examines the evolving legal tensions between platform liability avoidance mechanisms and indirect participation in unlawful digital activities facilitated through third-party uploaded content. Contemporary digital platforms increasingly operate through algorithmically mediated ecosystems in which user-generated content becomes economically valuable through engagement optimization, targeted dissemination, and platform monetization structures. While safe harbor doctrines were originally developed to protect intermediaries lacking direct editorial control over user activity, contemporary platform architectures increasingly blur the distinction between passive hosting and active participation. This study analyzes the structural limitations of safe harbor protections within transnational digital environments characterized by algorithmic amplification, recommendation systems, behavioral optimization, and monetized engagement infrastructures. Through comparative doctrinal analysis integrating intermediary liability theory, digital governance frameworks, and platform accountability models, the paper argues that contemporary safe harbor regimes inadequately address indirect forms of platform participation that contribute to the dissemination, amplification, and normalization of unlawful content. The study concludes that emerging digital ecosystems require revised legal standards capable of distinguishing genuinely neutral intermediaries from algorithmically interventionist platforms operating through economically incentivized visibility systems.

detail.abstract: Generative AI gives creative works a dual role as final goods and training inputs. This dual role creates an appropriation problem: copyrighted knowledge strengthens AI and supports content production through nonrival AI use, but infringing use of such knowledge erodes returns to original creation. We develop a general equilibrium model with an upstream AI sector, an original sector, and a derivative sector. In the decentralized equilibrium, labor is underallocated to original production and overallocated to AI production because private agents do not internalize the cross-sector effects of nonrival AI use and the knowledge spillovers embedded in AI training; the derivative sector's AI use creates no separate distortion. We examine two governance instruments: digital taxation and copyright litigation. Optimal taxation is asymmetric: the derivative sector is always taxed, while the original and AI sectors may be taxed or subsidized depending on the strength of appropriation and the value of AI as a nonrival input. Copyright litigation has an inverted-U welfare effect: moderate enforcement reallocates returns toward original creators through a beneficial compensation effect, whereas excessive enforcement contracts AI supply and downstream output through an adverse production effect. The optimal policy depends on the relative costs of tax administration and legal enforcement.

detail.abstract: Cryptocurrency has emerged as a disruptive force in global financial systems, presenting both transformative opportunities and multifaceted challenges for developing economies. This paper presents a narrative literature review examining the landscape of cryptocurrency awareness, adoption, and regulation in Bangladesh-a lower-middle-income economy ranked among the world's top remittance recipients and freelancing nations. Drawing on peer-reviewed literature, policy documents, and institutional reports published between 2020 and 2025, we analyse the interplay between informal adoption, regulatory ambiguity, and macro-financial vulnerabilities. Our review synthesises evidence from four thematic domains: (i) the socioeconomic drivers of grassroots cryptocurrency adoption; (ii) the role of stablecoins and decentralised finance (DeFi) in supporting remittances and freelance income; (iii) the governance and consumer-protection failures that have enabled large-scale fraud; and (iv) the emerging policy discourse surrounding Central Bank Digital Currencies (CBDCs) and blockchain governance frameworks. We find that despite a formal regulatory prohibition, Bangladesh has developed a substantial and growing crypto user base, driven primarily by economic necessity rather than speculative intent. The paper concludes by proposing a contextually appropriate regulatory pathway grounded in comparative international evidence, and identifies gaps that warrant primary empirical investigation.

title: Failures in Marginal Reasoning under Nonlinear Incentives *

detail.title: Failures in Marginal Reasoning under Nonlinear Incentives *
detail.abstract: Despite the central role of marginal reasoning in economic theory, individuals frequently make mistakes under nonlinear incentives. I develop an elicitation framework that separates subjects' knowledge of the optimal rule of marginal reasoning from their implementation of the rule in decisions under piecewise-linear tax schedules. In a 2 × 2 experiment, I vary schedule complexity along two dimensions, the total tax brackets in the schedule and the number of marginal tax rate-slopes relevant to optimal decision. Perfect rule-knowledge is rare even under full disclosure of the schedule, as only 21.2% of subjects answer all questions correctly on a basic rule-knowledge check. However, error levels remain high even among such subjects. 86.3% of the overall average error in the sample persists in the average error of perfect rule-knowers, reflecting an upper bound on implementation frictions beyond lack of knowledge. Complexity reshapes the mapping between rule-knowledge and decision quality, as the performance gap between perfect and imperfect rule-knowers is wider in less complex environments, in particular, mixed environments where only one of the two dimensions of schedule complexity is higher. The results highlight distinct cognitive failures in marginal reasoning and their sensitivity to the complexity of the incentive.

detail.title: Generative Artificial Intelligence and the Doctrine of Fair Use: A Critical Analysis of Nepal's Copyright Framework
detail.abstract: The rapid proliferation of generative artificial intelligence (AI) systems has exposed a profound and largely unaddressed lacuna in Nepal's intellectual property law. This article critically examines whether the fair use doctrine enshrined in Section 16 of the Copyright Act, 2059 (2002) is adequate to address the multifaceted legal challenges posed by generative AIspecifically regarding the use of copyrighted works as training data and the copyright status of AI-generated outputs. Employing a doctrinal and comparative methodology, the article analyses Nepal's statutory framework against those of the United States, the United Kingdom, India, and Cambodia. The analysis reveals that Nepal's closed-list fair dealing model, its anthropocentric definition of authorship, and its absence of a transformative-use standard collectively render the existing legal regime structurally inadequate for the digital age. The article concludes with targeted normative recommendations for legislative reform, judicial capacity-building, and institutional modernization, proposing a hybrid fair-use model and the introduction of surrogate authorship provisions as immediate priorities.

title: Deterrence Redefined: The Backfire Mechanism in Recognition Structures

detail.title: Deterrence Redefined: The Backfire Mechanism in Recognition Structures
detail.abstract: Deterrence may simultaneously generate stabilization and the conditions for breakdown. This study redefines the condition under which deterrence is established not as a mere equilibrium of power or utility, but as a condition of structural consistency within the internal structure of subjective recognition under interaction. From this perspective, deterrent action is reformulated not as a process in which stability cumulatively increases through the accumulation of measures, but as an antinomic structure in which intervention itself may simultaneously induce stabilization and reverse effects (backfire). The central proposition of this study is that such backfire effects are not merely the result of misperception or accidental failure, but arise endogenously from recognition structures under conditions of uncertainty. Previous studies have individually refined such elements as utility evaluation, mutual recognition, and the institutional and organizational conditions constraining behavior within different theoretical traditions. However, they have not systematically explained how these elements are interconnected, nor how different behavioral outcomes and unintended escalation may emerge under the same conditions. In response to this theoretical gap, this study elucidates the multilayered recognition structure and its internal mechanisms, thereby providing a unified theoretical framework for explaining not only the establishment, incomplete fulfillment, and breakdown of deterrence, but also the branching processes of behavior, including reverse effects.

title: Rational Stein Operator Based Dynamic Risk Modeling and Early Warning for Financial Heavy-Tailed Assets Author Information

detail.title: Rational Stein Operator Based Dynamic Risk Modeling and Early Warning for Financial Heavy-Tailed Assets Author Information
detail.abstract:
This paper develops a dynamic risk modeling and early warning framework for extremelyheavy-tailed financial assets such as Bitcoin. We propose the Rational Stein Operator toendogenously generate power-law tails and achieve decoupling of skewness and tail parameters. Based on the Stein identity, we construct a Bounded Generalized Methodof Moments (Bounded GMM) estimator that remains consistent under the weak conditionof only the first moment existing (ν < 0.5), avoiding the calculation of normalization constantsand the failure of traditional estimators under infinite kurtosis.
Using daily returns of Bitcoin, S&P 500, and WTI crude oil from 2018 to 2025, we showthat the model accurately captures time-varying tail dynamics. At the 99.9%confidence level, itsVaR backtesting performance significantly outperforms Gaussian and static Student’s t models, and its computational efficiency exceeds GARCH-EVT. Furthermore, the dynamictail parameter ν_t serves as an effective indicator for identifying macro liquidity inflection points and systemic risk shifts, providing reliable early warning signals ahead of market crashes.
This study offers a theoretically rigorous and practically feasible approach to extreme riskmanagement for heavy-tailed financial assets, suitable for financial risk measurement, regulatory monitoring, and macroprudential applications.

detail.abstract: This paper produces the first estimates of local damages from climate change, reflecting heterogeneous exposure and responses to climate for ∼25,000 globally comprehensive regions. Global damages from a marginal ton of CO 2 emissions (i.e., the social cost of carbon) are $336 (2025 USD), with just 5% occurring in OECD countries that account for half of historical emissions. Restricting to country-level analysis obscures half the variation in local damages. Despite large benefits from adaptation and modest average impacts, 7% of world population experiences annually recurring Great Recession level damages by 2100 under business-as-usual warming. These findings illustrate climate change's marked inequality.

detail.abstract: Recent enthusiasm for field experiments, and especially for natural field experiments (NFEs), in which subjects go about their daily activities unaware that any study is taking place, has sometimes been read as a verdict against the laboratory. I argue that such a verdict is wrong. Through the lens of a simple rational-choice model, I show that the four standard experimental designs (laboratory, artefactual field experiment (AFE), framed field experiment (FFE), and NFE) are comparative-static restrictions of one maximization problem, each identifying a parameter the others cannot. The model reveals that each design type has distinctive strengths and weaknesses across various dimensions of knowledge creation, including the enforcement of the conditions for causal identification, the faithfulness of the experimental environment to the theory being tested, the identification of economic primitives via theoretical structure, and the ethics of studying human subjects. On each of the dimensions, the four design types are complements rather than rivals. Nowhere is this complementarity more evident than between the two extremes. The lab enforces the conditions for causal identification that the NFE must inherit from the market; the NFE recovers the parameter that governs behaviour in the wild, free of the selection, scrutiny, and environmental distortions the lab cannot escape. A research programme using all four designs together demonstrates something no single design can produce. The framework further accommodates the recent rise of online and survey experiments as natural extensions. Our discipline's recent drift away from laboratory evidence is leaving an important structural gap that natural field experiments, however well conceived, cannot fill.

publicationDetails.detailsText: University of Chicago, Becker Friedman Institute for Economics Working Paper No. 2026-85
publicationDetails.journalName: Becker Friedman Institute for Economics Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: How does uncertainty about future government policy affect households' beliefs and subsequent borrowing, spending and debt payment behavior? We study these questions through the lens of student loan forgiveness in the United States, which following electoral promises, was announced in 2022 but never implemented due to judicial rulings. We conduct a customized information provision experiment embedded in a survey eliciting real-time beliefs about future debt forgiveness and repayment, which we link to credit bureau data, employment verification data, and nondurables consumption. Eligible borrowers who are more optimistic about forgiveness reduce payments on student loans by \$40 per month and increase non-durable spending by $100 per month. We also find some evidence optimistic borrowers may postpone durable spending waiting for uncertainty to resolve. Borrowers optimistic about future payment pauses make fewer payments on their student loans, reduce payment by $40 per month and are 7.5 percentage points more likely to be delinquent after payments resume. A quantification exercise finds welfare losses from incorrect beliefs can exceed 43 percent of the initial loan balance. Our results provide micro-evidence on the role of policy uncertainty in household decision-making, and have implications for government announcements and commitment policy.

title: Bayesian Causal Estimation of Germany's Recent Fuel Price Policy: The High Noon Rule and the 2026 Fuel Tax Discount
affiliations: RWI  Leibniz Institute for Economic Research , RWI - Leibniz Institute for Economic Research and RWI - Leibniz Institute for Economic Research

detail.title: Bayesian Causal Estimation of Germany's Recent Fuel Price Policy: The High Noon Rule and the 2026 Fuel Tax Discount

publicationDetails.journalName: United States Association for Energy Economics (USAEE) & International Association for Energy Economics (IAEE) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: In April 2026, the German government introduced the High Noon Rule, restricting fuel stations to a single permitted daily price increase at midday. Four weeks later, a two-month tax discount cut the fuel duty by €0.167 per litre. Using a Bayesian Structural Time Series model, we estimate the causal impact of each measure on retail prices. The High Noon Rule had no discernible effect on diesel, yet raised petrol prices by nearly 5 cents. Consistent with a competitive market, the tax discount was largely passed through to consumers.

title: How Do Financial and Longevity Literacy Affect Annuity Demand?
affiliations: University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign - Department of Finance

detail.title: How Do Financial and Longevity Literacy Affect Annuity Demand?
detail.abstract:
Deciding whether to use an annuity to draw down accumulated retirement wealth is among the most complex financial decisions individuals face. It requires reasoning about longevity risk, stochastic income streams, and largely irreversible tradeoffs, often at older ages and with limited opportunities to learn from experience. This paper reviews theoretical, empirical, and experimental research to examine how financial literacy and longevity literacy shape annuitization decisions. While some extensions of the standard lifecycle model can rationalize low annuity demand, their explanatory power depends on individuals’ ability to optimize over a set of complex risks and tradeoffs. Evidence shows that, although financial and longevity literacy are only weakly and inconsistently related to annuity take-up, they are strongly associated with retirement planning, the coherence of annuity valuations, and sensitivity to framing and choice architecture. These patterns suggest that literacy should be understood not as a direct determinant of annuity demand, but as a constraint on the extent to which observed annuitization behavior can be interpreted as revealing true preferences.

title: The Female Sensitivity Hypothesis: Evidence From Experimental Economics
affiliations: Lehigh University, University of Richmond - E. Claiborne Robins School of Business - Economics and University of Pittsburgh - Department of Economics

detail.title: The Female Sensitivity Hypothesis: Evidence From Experimental Economics
detail.abstract:
We assess the empirical evidence for the hypothesis that women more than men respond to changes in treatment. First, we examine whether the results of over two hundred experimental economics papers support the female sensitivity hypothesis. Second, using data from two studies (DellaVigna and Pope, 2022; Exley et al., 2025), we conduct over two hundred pairwise tests of the hypothesis. Both analyses show that gender is not predictive of responsiveness to treatment. We further examine how the hypothesis has been disseminated in the literature and find that it is referenced predominantly by papers that support it.

detail.abstract: Since early 2025, the Korean won (KRW) has faced persistent downward pressure, exhibiting a pronounced weakness against major currencies, with the notable exception of the Japanese yen. For the first time in history, the annual average KRW/USD exchange rate has breached the 1,400 level. This surpasses the average rates seen during the Asian Financial Crisis (1,395 won in 1998) and the Global Financial Crisis (1,276 won in 2009). Consequently, speculative concerns regarding a potential currency crisis have emerged within domestic media. Having experienced the trauma of the 1997 Asian Financial Crisis and the 2008 Global Financial Crisis, South Korea remains sensitive to such volatility. This report compares the current situation with these past crises to assess the risk level and delineate policy imperatives for FX market stability. (The rest omitted.)

title: Dynamic Risk Adjustment in Markets with Persistent Risk and Manipulable Signals: Market Design for Health Insurance

detail.title: Dynamic Risk Adjustment in Markets with Persistent Risk and Manipulable Signals: Market Design for Health Insurance
detail.abstract:
Risk adjustment is a payment mechanism, not only a prediction problem. I extend optimal risk adjustment to dynamic insurance markets in which plans capture future residuals from persistent risk. Under an efficiency criterion, payments should reflect expected profits and losses over the enrollee relationship on margins plans control, not only one-year spending predictions. A finite-cell model separates selection, health production, and manipulable measurement. The framework implies that annual recalculation can tax prevention, high-R2 prediction can reduce welfare, and lagged claims anchors are useful only with gaming safeguards.

title: Climate Risks and Private Infrastructure Valuation
affiliations: EDHEC Business School and EDHEC Business School

detail.title: Climate Risks and Private Infrastructure Valuation

publicationDetails.journalName: BAFFI Centre on Economics, Finance & Regulation Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper examines how climate-related news affects the cost of capital for private infrastructure investment across countries. We combine a novel dataset of global infrastructure transactions with country-level measures of climate sentiment constructed from GDELT news data, alongside indicators of climate policy stringency and physical risk. We find that climate-related information is systematically incorporated into asset valuations: more adverse climate news is associated with lower valuation multiples, consistent with higher required returns, while more favorable news increases valuations. In contrast, we find no significant effects on realized returns, suggesting that climate information primarily operates through ex-ante adjustments in discount rates rather than realized cash flows. The effects are stronger in countries with higher transition risk and weaker institutional environments. These findings highlight the role of information in shaping financing conditions and suggest that climate-related narratives can influence the allocation of capital during the energy transition by affecting the cost of infrastructure investment.

title: A Cohort Perspective on Latin America's Fertility Transition
affiliations: University of California, San Diego (UCSD) - University of California, San Diego and University of California, San Diego (UCSD)

detail.title: A Cohort Perspective on Latin America's Fertility Transition
detail.abstract:
Latin America's momentous fertility transition is now in the domain of history, allowing a cohort perspective on the decline of completed fertility. Using census microdata from 17 Latin American countries, we track female birth cohorts from the 1920s to the 1970s by subnational region to document the extent to which cohort fertility decline coincided with other demographic and socioeconomic processes. Across cohorts within subnational regions, children ever born fell one-for-one with mortality decline. Expansions in urbanization, multigenerational living, women's and husbands' education, women's employment, and the non-agricultural sector all predicted declines in ever-born and surviving fertility, but women's education and sectoral composition were the dominant forces after covariate adjustment. Fertility decline was not systematically linked with improvements in children's outcomes, including school enrollment, literacy, primary completion, and non-employment. These cohort facts challenge theories of fertility decline centered on women's work and children's education but support others emphasizing women's education.

title: 'Nobody Wants to Work Anymore': Lifetime Labor Market Experiences and the Decline of Male LFP in the United States

detail.title: 'Nobody Wants to Work Anymore': Lifetime Labor Market Experiences and the Decline of Male LFP in the United States
detail.abstract:
Male labor force participation has declined steadily for 50 years in the United States. We show that one cause has been changes in men's beliefs about the returns to work, shaped by lifetime experiences of the aggregate male labor market. We find that experience effects on participation persist for men who move across state lines, are stronger for same-race male experiences, and are driven by formative childhood years. We also document effects of experiences on direct measures of labor market expectations. Our findings suggest that experience effects can turn short-run declines in labor demand into long-run declines in labor supply.

title: Dollar Erosion: Understanding the Loss of Reserve Currency Status
affiliations: , Stanford Graduate School of Business, Stanford University and New York University (NYU) - Department of Finance

detail.title: Dollar Erosion: Understanding the Loss of Reserve Currency Status
detail.abstract:
We quantify the impact of the loss of reserve currency status in goods and asset markets. In goods markets, the loss of seigniorage (1% of GDP per annum) makes American households spend less, mostly on U.S. goods, leaving an excess supply of U.S. goods to be cleared by a real depreciation of the dollar. The larger the home bias and the lower the elasticity of substitution between home and foreign goods, the larger the required depreciation. Standard parameters imply an 8.8% real depreciation of the dollar. In asset markets, about 50% of GDP in dollar bonds must be reabsorbed by home investors, raising the U.S. real interest rate. Standard parameters imply a 90 basis points rise, leading to an aggregate wealth loss of roughly one year of U.S. GDP.

title: Reconciling Micro Elasticities with the Macro Decline in Labor Supply
affiliations: University of Minnesota - Minneapolis

detail.title: Reconciling Micro Elasticities with the Macro Decline in Labor Supply
detail.abstract:
Micro estimates of the Marshallian elasticity of labor supply are small and typically positive, whereas cross-country and time-series patterns of hours imply a strong negative relationship between wages and hours. I reconcile these two apparently contradictory observations using a single utility specification and taking into account heterogeneity in non-labor income. Micro estimates condition on non-labor income, while macro variation allows capital income to adjust alongside labor income, which strengthens the income effect. A model with heterogeneous households and exogenous capital income yields closed-form expressions in which the distribution of the labor share shapes the gap between the micro and the macro elasticities. A cross-sectional regression of hours on wages that conditions on the labor share recovers the macro elasticity. A dynamic model with heterogeneous households and incomplete asset markets reproduces both elasticities as outcomes when disciplined by joint moments of wages, hours, consumption, and wealth. The income effects that bridge the gap between the two elasticities imply marginal propensities to earn that lie in the range of estimates of micro studies on lottery winners.

title: The Ghost in the Index: Knowledge Exclusion and the Fallacy of the Low-Resource Label: A Position Paper

detail.title: The Ghost in the Index: Knowledge Exclusion and the Fallacy of the Low-Resource Label: A Position Paper

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No conflict of interest

detail.abstract: The term low-resource languages is now widely used in machine intelligence to describe languages with limited digital data, annotated corpora, and processing tools. Yet this label hides major scientific, social, and methodological problems. It defines languages and communities by what they supposedly lack instead of recognizing their knowledge systems, communicative richness, memory structures, and cultural complexity. The term also obscures the historical, economic, and political causes of digital exclusion, including colonial infrastructures, unequal funding, platform concentration, and selective technological investment. In practice, many current machine intelligence pipelines are designed around written text and standardized orthographies, often relying on dominant databases and benchmarks that privilege text-only formats while excluding oral, gestural, performative, and multimodal forms of communication. As a result, they fail to process forms of communication that are central to many audioliterate populations, including oral narratives, prosody, rhythm, intonation, gesture, mimicry, facial expression, silence, and collective interaction. Current text-centered architectures remain poorly adapted to direct textless audio-to-audio systems, despite the fact that such pipelines are essential for communities where knowledge transmission is primarily oral. This limitation reflects a broader absence of sensory machine intelligence capable of integrating sound, embodiment, context, and multimodal social meaning. The label also encourages extractive forms of research in which communities are treated mainly as sources of raw data, often without reciprocity, long-term collaboration, or local technological benefit. The term lacks operational precision. It fails to distinguish between data scarcity, absence of digital infrastructure, exclusion from dominant technological systems, and sociopolitical marginalization. A more rigorous and community-centered vocabulary is therefore necessary for scientifically accurate and multi-scale ethically responsible research.

title: Before the Exodus? Young Scientists and the Future of US Science
affiliations: Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) - Sloan School of Management, Harvard University - Strategy Unit and Monash University

detail.title: Before the Exodus? Young Scientists and the Future of US Science
detail.abstract:
Shortly after major policy changes to US science funding began in early 2025, we surveyed 916 young biomedical scientists – PhD students and postdoctoral researchers – about their career intentions and expectations. The results document a dramatic shift in sentiment. Barely half of respondents now say they are likely to remain in academia, down 22 percentage points from how they felt six months earlier. The fraction likely to stay in the United States fell by 21 percentage points. Even satisfaction with having pursued a PhD in science declined by 16 percentage points. These are not the complaints of established scientists defending their budgets, but rather the stated intentions of the next generation – the scientists who would, in ordinary times, become the principal investigators of the future.

title: Buddhist Economics as a Blueprint for a Post-Capitalist Circular World
affiliations: Global College (Malta), Global College (Malta)

detail.title: Buddhist Economics as a Blueprint for a Post-Capitalist Circular World
detail.abstract: Modern macroeconomic paradigms, rooted in Western classical theory, prioritize maximal consumption and physical growth at the expense of ecological stability. This paper examines the historical trajectory of this environmental crisis, from Adam Smith's growth-centric foundations to the modern globalized economy's contribution to climate change. Recognizing the structural failures of both capitalist exploitation and historical socialist alternatives, this study proposes Buddhist economics as a necessary psychological and structural alternative. By replacing the goal of maximal consumption with optimal well-being, Buddhist economics aligns seamlessly with the modern framework of the circular economy. Through a case study of Bhutan's Gross National Happiness (GNH) and carbon-negative initiatives, alongside a comparative empirical analysis of GNH and GDP frameworks, this paper argues that true sustainable development requires an internal shift in human consciousness rather than mere cosmetic regulatory adjustments.

title: Pollinator Decline Reveals Uneven Impacts From Climate-driven Biodiversity Loss
affiliations: Ca Foscari University of Venice, Università degli Studi di Milano and Ca’ Foscari University of Venice

detail.title: Pollinator Decline Reveals Uneven Impacts From Climate-driven Biodiversity Loss

declarations.funderStatement: This work was supported by the European Union’s Assessing Climate Change Risk in EUrope (ACCREU) project (Grant Agreement No. 101081358; Funding scheme: HORIZON-CL5-2022-D1-07-two-stage).

detail.abstract:
Ecosystems and biodiversity sustain human welfare through essential services such as pollination, collectively contributing a significant proportion to global GDP. Yet their representation in long-term socioeconomic projections remains critically limited, leading to biased outlooks, particularly under accelerating environmental change. 

Here we develop the first long-term, climate-driven evaluation of pollination impacts, integrating biophysical and economic modelling of wild pollinator species and 129 crops to quantify how biodiversity loss propagates through agricultural systems into the macro-economy across 122 EU sub-national regions to 2070.

EU-wide average impacts, showing GDP losses up to €57.7 billion/year (-0.18\%) and agricultural sector losses of -1.5 to -6.0\% by 2070, systematically conceal severe spatial concentration of damages. Under high-emission scenarios, cropland productivity losses for vegetables, fruits and nuts reach -25.5\% in the most exposed regions, with sectorial economic impacts spanning between -21.35\% and +8.85\%. Mediterranean and eastern EU regions bear disproportionate burdens, amplifying intra-EU economic disparities. 

Our findings highlight the spatial heterogeneity of pollination decline and its uneven effects on pollinator-dependent crops across regions, revealing critical vulnerabilities in the agricultural systems. These results demonstrate that biodiversity impacts cannot be properly captured by national-scale assessments and that spatial resolution is not a technical choice but a determinant of whether risks are visible at all. Standard integrated assessment models, typically resolved at macro-regional level, may systematically underestimate the vulnerability to climate-biodiversity impacts as aggregation conceals distributional tails by factors of 2-5×.

title: Calibrated but Not Sharp: Stated Probabilities in Five-Minute Crypto Markets on Polymarket

detail.title: Calibrated but Not Sharp: Stated Probabilities in Five-Minute Crypto Markets on Polymarket
detail.abstract: When a prediction market shows a high chance, does the event happen that often, or is the price fooling you? This paper studies that for five-minute, USDC-denominated up/down contracts on Polymarket, across Bitcoin, Ether, Solana, and Dogecoin, and reports three findings. First, the prices are calibrated. Using a clean logger that records the implied probability of every active market at a fixed moment about a minute before close, whether or not anyone traded it, I obtain 14,808 contracts over sixteen days, and stated probabilities match realized frequencies to within about one percentage point across the range, including in the extreme tails. The slope of realized outcomes on stated probability is 1.01, and three small-sample methods built for sixteen day-clusters, a wild-cluster bootstrap, an Ibragimov-Muller test, and randomization inference, all fail to reject the value of 1.0; the intervals are wide enough that only a favorite-longshot bias larger than a few percent in slope terms is ruled out. This is reassuring but unsurprising, since a liquid market should price roughly like this. Second, and more useful as method, a separate large but selected dataset of about 209,000 trade entries shows how easily this can be gotten wrong: treating those correlated trades as independent manufactures a statistically significant favorite-longshot bias that vanishes under dependence-robust inference and is absent from the clean data. Third, calibration is not sharpness. The posted probabilities hug fifty-fifty even when the near-term outcome is largely decided. A costless rule that asks only which side is ahead at the snapshot calls the final direction about 81 percent of the time against the market's 64 percent, with more than double the Brier resolution, and this survives rebuilding the rule on a second, independent exchange feed. I therefore report the discrimination of the posted quote as low relative to freely available information, and stop short of calling it trader underreaction, because the logged value is a non-executable quote on a thin market and I have no spread or order-book data to rule out microstructure. Two limits bound everything: sixteen days on a single venue, and a deliberately extreme five-minute horizon.

title: The Closing Externality Window: First-Principles Sustainability and the Evidence for a Compressing Externality Lag

detail.title: The Closing Externality Window: First-Principles Sustainability and the Evidence for a Compressing Externality Lag

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is the founder of SustBridge AI, a sustainability-analytics company. SustBridge had no role in the design, data collection, analysis, or conclusions of this study, and the findings are not contingent on any commercial interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable — the study analyses publicly documented historical corporate cases; no human participants were involved.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: Corporate sustainability is conventionally argued by analogy — such as the performance of ESG funds, regulatory pressure, or consumer sentiment — and each such argument weakens as its underlying condition shifts. This paper instead documents a measurable empirical regularity and rebuilds the case for sustainability on it, as a problem in capital allocation rather than values. The evidence is a purpose-built dataset of 39 historical and contemporary cases, spanning 167 years of origination dates (1850–2017). The cases cover all three ESG pillars, admitted under a two-track materiality rule and balanced by pre-specified geographic, sector, and historical-depth guards. Across them, the latency to crystallisation has compressed at about two-thirds of a year per calendar year of origination (R² = 0.737, p < 0.0001). The relationship holds within each ESG pillar and across sensitivity tests, and is, if anything, conservative against right-censoring. Read economically, the window during which a cost can remain an unpriced externality is closing: externalities are internalised faster than they once were, and the mechanisms doing the compressing are largely non-legislative. From four first-principles premises the paper derives this claim, situates the empirical result within it, and organises the implications into a staged account — the First-Principles Sustainability flywheel — of how a compressing externality lag enters capital-allocation decisions of every kind, with project-finance and merger-and-acquisition due diligence its most immediate application. Two instruments that operationalise its central stages — a time-to-internalisation duration model and a breaking-point function for the act-versus-defer decision — are developed in a companion paper.

title: DSP-Assisted Deep Learning for Transmission Line Fault Detection in Smart Grids Under Clean and Noisy Conditions
affiliations: City University

detail.title: DSP-Assisted Deep Learning for Transmission Line Fault Detection in Smart Grids Under Clean and Noisy Conditions
detail.abstract: This paper presents a deep learning-based fault detection system for smart grid transmission lines, addressing the critical need for robust and accurate fault identification to ensure grid stability and reliability. The proposed methodology integrates Digital Signal Processing (DSP) techniques for comprehensive feature extraction from raw current and voltage signals. Key DSP features, including instantaneous zero-sequence components, total magnitudes, and maximum instantaneous values, were derived to characterize various fault conditions. A multi-layer perceptron (MLP) deep learning model was then developed and trained on these engineered features.On a clean dataset, the model achieved exceptional performance with a test accuracy of 99.72%, and near-perfect precision, recall, and F1-scores of 1.00 for both fault and no-fault classes, as evidenced by a confusion matrix showing only 5 misclassifications out of 1801 samples. To assess robustness, the system was further evaluated using data augmented with Gaussian noise (mean=0, std=0.1). When retrained and tested on noisy data, the model maintained high performance, achieving a test accuracy of 99.22% and consistent precision, recall, and F1-scores of 0.99 across classes. This demonstrates the model's resilience to typical measurement uncertainties. The findings underscore the efficacy of combining DSP-engineered features with deep learning for highly accurate and robust fault detection in complex smart grid environments.

title: The Information-Survival Ratio: A Within-Strategy Diagnostic of Conditioning Overfit in Walk-Forward Backtests
affiliations: University of Reading

detail.title: The Information-Survival Ratio: A Within-Strategy Diagnostic of Conditioning Overfit in Walk-Forward Backtests

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interest. The views expressed in this paper are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect those of Miralta Finance Bank, S.A.
declarations.funderStatement: This work received no external funding.

detail.abstract: When a researcher tests a conditional trading strategy in-sample using a rich set of conditioning variables, in-sample performance typically exceeds walk-forward performance. Existing diagnostics for this gap operate across strategies multiple-testing corrections that adjust observed Sharpe ratios for the implicit search across many candidate strategies. They are silent on a second source of overfitting that occurs within a single strategy: how much of the conditioning information used in-sample also survives walk-forward selection. We propose the information-survival ratio (ISR), a within-strategy diagnostic that addresses this second source. The researcher first specifies how much conditioning information to use in-sample, expressed as a Kullback-Leibler divergence from the unconditional benchmark. The diagnostic then asks how much of this budget walk-forward cross-validation keeps out-of-sample. A high ratio means the conditioning information survives; a low ratio means walk-forward reverts to the unconditional benchmark. We develop selection inference for the cross-fitted walk-forward argmax: a temporal buffer criterion, an exponential large-deviation rate under mixing and fixed positive separation, stationary block bootstrap validity, and a joint specification-budget extension. An application across equity, hedge fund, industry, and single-name panels finds that information survival varies substantially across asset classes, with hedge fund indices generally retaining the largest fraction of conditioning capacity.

title: Incomplete Gamma Representations of the Riemann Xi Function: a Thorin Bernstein Framework
affiliations: University of Chicago - Booth School of Business

detail.title: Incomplete Gamma Representations of the Riemann Xi Function: a Thorin Bernstein Framework
detail.abstract: We study the analytic continuation of the completed zeta function ξ through its incomplete gamma representation and develop a probabilistic framework for it based on Thorin measures, generalized gamma convolutions (GGC) and hyperbolic complete monotonicity (HCM). The incomplete gamma form keeps the Gaussian building blocks of the theta function intact under continuation, which exposes a two tier structure: a trivial tier indexed by the squares πn 2 , which is unconditionally a ThorinBernstein subordinator and a GGC; and a nontrivial tier indexed by the squared ordinates  of the zeros, which is a GGC if and only if the Riemann Hypothesis holds. We give four equivalent faces of this equivalence (Thorin positivity, Thorin Bernstein, Stieltjes transform, and complete monotonicity of the Lévy density), a Hankel determinant (secondary zeta) moment criterion in the spirit of Li and Voros, and an explicit Jacobi theta density for the trivial tier. We survey the incomplete gamma representations of Lavrik Paris Cang, Haglund, and CrandallCoey, and read the latter inside the Thorin framework. Using Steutel's infinite divisibility criterion the engine of Kristiansen's proof that mixtures of Γ(α) are infinitely divisible i α ≤ 2we show that the incomplete gamma is a truncated stable Bernstein function, that truncation is exactly the GGC→ID gap, and we prove a new stable 1 2 multiplier theorem dual to Kristiansen's at the sharp HCM threshold. The exposition is self-contained and the analytic identities are veried numerically.

title: Digital Identity, Data Justice, and Human Capabilities: A Technology Impact Assessment of Uganda's National Identification System

detail.title: Digital Identity, Data Justice, and Human Capabilities: A Technology Impact Assessment of Uganda's National Identification System

detail.abstract:
Digital identity systems have emerged as a foundational component of Digital Public Infrastructure (DPI) and are increasingly promoted as instruments for improving service delivery, enhancing financial inclusion, strengthening state capacity, and advancing Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) 16.9 on legal identity for all. Despite growing investment in national digital identity systems across Africa, existing scholarship remains divided between studies emphasizing developmental benefits and those highlighting risks of exclusion, surveillance, and governance failures. Few studies integrate these perspectives within a comprehensive Technology Impact Assessment (TIA) framework.

This paper applies a Technology Impact Assessment framework to evaluate Uganda's National Identification System and its implications for inclusion, human capabilities, and data justice. Drawing on Technology Impact Assessment scholarship, the Capability Approach, and Data Justice theory, the study examines how digital identity systems shape access to services, opportunities, and rights among different population groups. The analysis is based on qualitative document analysis of legal frameworks, policy documents, academic literature, civil society reports, and empirical studies relating to Uganda's digital identity ecosystem.

The findings indicate that Uganda's National Identification System has generated important benefits in civil identification, administrative coordination, financial inclusion, and service delivery. However, these benefits are unevenly distributed and accompanied by significant challenges, including registration barriers, exclusion of vulnerable populations, privacy concerns, governance weaknesses, and increasing dependency on digital identity for access to public services. Women, older persons, rural populations, and individuals lacking supporting documentation face disproportionate risks of exclusion. The analysis further demonstrates that the developmental value of digital identity systems cannot be assessed solely through enrollment rates or technical performance but must also consider their effects on substantive freedoms, participation, and equitable access to opportunities.

The paper contributes to scholarship on digital identity and Digital Public Infrastructure by integrating Technology Impact Assessment, the Capability Approach, and Data Justice into a single analytical framework. It argues that digital identity systems should be evaluated not only as technological infrastructures but also as governance and development infrastructures whose success depends on their ability to expand human capabilities, minimize exclusion, promote data justice, and support rights-based digital governance.

title: Beyond Mean-Variance: Goal-Based Portfolio Optimisation with Derivatives and Structured Products

detail.title: Beyond Mean-Variance: Goal-Based Portfolio Optimisation with Derivatives and Structured Products

declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This research did not involve human participants, animals, or personal data.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: This paper documents a research optimiser that builds goal-based portfolios beyond the classical mean-variance frame. It re-implements and extends a 2012 MSc thesis (USI Lugano) that replicated the mental-accounting models of Das & Statman (2009) and Das, Markowitz, Scheid & Statman (2010). Two engines are provided: an exact grid optimiser that reproduces the thesis results on a discretised state space, and a scalable Monte-Carlo + CVaR optimiser that escapes the curse of dimensionality through copula scenarios and a linear program. Both price derivatives and structured products arbitrage-consistently, and an out-of-sample backtest holds the chosen portfolio on later, unseen data. Beyond a faithful re-implementation, the paper records two substantive corrections relative to the thesis-the enforcement of the Expected-Shortfall constraint and the fair pricing of structured notes-and reports results, validation and limitations.
