title: Platforms and Antitrust: What Amex Could Learn from Microsoft
affiliations: Cornell University - Law School

detail.title: Platforms and Antitrust: What Amex Could Learn from Microsoft

publicationDetails.journalName: Cornell Law School Legal Studies Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
The economics of multi-sided platforms has important implications for antitrust. In its 2018 Amex decision, the Supreme Court held that, in cases involving "transaction platforms," the market must be defined to include both sides. Under this rule, a plaintiff cannot prove anticompetitive harm by showing a reduction in competition and welfare on one side; it must show a net harm across both sides combined. The Amex majority viewed this as necessary to account for indirect network effects, which create interdependence between the two sides of a platform. 

However, 25 years ago, Microsoft did precisely what Amex said was impossible: it carefully accounted for the interdependence between the consumers and software developers on an operating system, despite defining the market around just the consumer side. It did this by considering how the challenged conduct affected developer activity (particularly multihoming) and then accounting for how this would feed back onto competition and welfare on the consumer side. 

The Amex majority conflated three questions: (1) whether courts should "consider" both sides; (2) whether antitrust should permit benefits on one side to excuse anticompetitive harm on the other; and (3) how to define the market. The economics of platforms answers the first question - we must indeed consider both sides. But the other two questions are independent, reflecting distinct normative and practical issues. Depending on the answers to those questions, there are three possible frameworks courts could use to evaluate platform conduct while accounting for the interdependence between sides. The Amex rule is unambiguously the most flawed and impractical option of the three. The Microsoft court avoided this problematic outcome because it understood not only that indirect network effects are important, but also how to account for them properly under the rule of reason.

title: Screwworms
affiliations: New York University (NYU), Department of Economics, Students

detail.title: Screwworms
detail.abstract: I show how farmers amplify the benefits of disease control in agriculture by changing their production techniques. Specifically, I examine the eradication of the screwworm, a deadly livestock parasite, in the southwestern United States. Exploiting spatial variation in infestation, I find that livestock production increased by 60 percent in initially heavily infested counties relative to less infested ones. This increase was driven by feedlot adoption, as farmers shifted to a technology which had been unviable under disease pressure. I estimate that this adaptation accounted for more than four-fifths of the total output gain.

title: Impact of COVID-19 on the Performance of Emerging Market Mutual Funds: Evidence From India
affiliations: TKM College of Arts and Science, Kollam 5

detail.title: Impact of COVID-19 on the Performance of Emerging Market Mutual Funds: Evidence From India
detail.abstract: The purpose of this paper is to examine the widely believed beating capacity of actively managed funds during the market downturn. This popular hypothesis has been tested with the performance of Indian Equity Mutual Funds during the pandemic period. The conditional alphas are estimated using lagged instrumental variables with the fixed effect/LSDV estimator and the sys-GMM estimator in contrast to the OLS estimation from a sample of 1271 schemes for 5 months from 1st March 2020 to 31st July 2020. The study's findings indicate that the actively managed Indian mutual fund co-moves with the market and does not possess the ability to beat the market. The major implication comes from the application of fixed effect and GMM estimators for the performance evaluation of Indian Mutual Funds' during the crisis period, and it serves the investors in deciding the profitable investment opportunities.

title: Barriers to Energy Transition in Indian Households: A Fuel-Stacking and Capability Approach Analysis Using NFHS-5 Data
affiliations: and Government of India - National Institute of Science Education and Research (NISER)

detail.title: Barriers to Energy Transition in Indian Households: A Fuel-Stacking and Capability Approach Analysis Using NFHS-5 Data
detail.abstract: India's shift from traditional to clean cooking fuels is vital for health, environmental, and development goals. Despite initiatives like Pradhan Mantri Ujjwala Yojana (PMUY), which distributed subsidized Liquefied Petroleum Gas (LPG) connections to over 50 million households, many rural and low-income households still rely on polluting fuels such as wood, cow dung, and crop residues. This study investigates structural, socioeconomic, and demographic barriers to the adoption of clean fuels using micro-level data from the National Family Health Survey (NFHS-5, 2019-21). A binary logistic regression model assesses how household education, caste, religion, housing quality, electricity access, and land ownership influence clean fuels use. Results show positive associations with education, urban residence, electricity access, and better housing, while agricultural land ownership and larger household size hinder adoption. Caste and religious disparities underscore social stratification's role. Strikingly, BPL card possession does not ensure clean fuel use, revealing subsidy programs' limits without behavioral or infrastructural support. We conclude that policies must extend beyond access to promote sustained usage. Recommendations include improving last-mile delivery, redesigning refill subsidies, and linking clean energy to welfare programs with behavior change campaigns for equitable, lasting transitions.

title: The Impact of Road Quality on Nearby House Prices
affiliations: West Virginia University - Department of Economics and Virginia Tech

detail.title: The Impact of Road Quality on Nearby House Prices
detail.abstract: This paper estimates the impact of road quality on house prices in Hamilton County, Ohio, USA which includes the city of Cincinnati. We use a hedonic regression framework using road segmentlevel international roughness index (IRI) data as a measure of road quality. We find that rougher roads decrease house prices, with a one standard deviation increase in road roughness from the sample mean decreasing house prices by 3.5%. This equates to a $6,700 decrease in the value of an average priced home in our sample, demonstrating the importance of road quality and maintenance for local economic development.

title: Co-Evolutionary Market Intelligence via Topological LLM-Agent Ensembles with Behavioural Non-Stationarity Adaptation

detail.title: Co-Evolutionary Market Intelligence via Topological LLM-Agent Ensembles with Behavioural Non-Stationarity Adaptation
detail.abstract: Financial markets are co-evolutionary systems: the strategies participants deploy reshape price dynamics, which in turn erode the very edges those strategies were built to exploit. This feedback is not distributional drift-the standard target of adaptive deep-learning methods-but strategic non-stationarity, a distinction that is, in our view, categorically more fundamental. No existing framework treats it as the primary design constraint. That gap motivates this work. We introduce the Co-Evolutionary Portfolio Policy (CEPP), an architecture that models markets as open-ended evolutionary games and constructs agents that adapt to the game's generative structure rather than its historical instances. Three modules constitute the system. First, a topological data analysis (TDA) pipeline constructs Vietoris-Rips filtrations over Bitcoin UTXO transaction graphs and limit-order-book depth profiles, vectorising persistence images stable under Hausdorff perturbation (Cohen-Steiner stability theorem); features empirically precede market dislocations by 2-3 trading days. Second, a chain-ofthought LLM reasoning layer converts macroeconomic narratives into Dirichlet-parameterised behavioural priors, injected as annealed KL-penalty constraints on the RL policy objective with confidence-gated hallucination guards; Theorem 2 establishes a formal bound on hallucination-induced policy divergence. Third, CR-EVO-a CMA-ES × PSO hybrid-minimises counterfactual regret against a best-response oracle, with a formal O ∆ f T log(N/δ) + εT regret bound (Theorem 1). Evaluated on equities, cryptocurrency, and commodity futures over a strict 2020-2024 out-of-sample window (1,258 trading days), CEPP achieves an annualised Sharpe ratio of 1.000 versus 0.761 for baseline PPO-DRL, with positive alpha across five structurally distinct regimes: the 2020 COVID crash, the 2020-21 recovery, the 2022 rate-hike cycle, the 2022 crypto winter, and the 2024 rate-reversal. TDA features alone improve baseline Sharpe from 0.761 to 0.863 (+13.4%), reproducible from public Blockchair data.

title: StreamShield: A Real-Time IoT Streaming Framework for Global Supply Chain Disruption Detection via Multi-Modal Data Fusion

detail.title: StreamShield: A Real-Time IoT Streaming Framework for Global Supply Chain Disruption Detection via Multi-Modal Data Fusion

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No competing interests
declarations.funderStatement: No one has funded this research

detail.abstract: Existing supply chain monitoring infrastructure is built for periodic reporting, not for the sub-day detection latency that modern disruptions demand. StreamShield closes this gap as a real-time IoT-style streaming framework that identifies and classifies supply chain disruptions through continuous fusion of seven heterogeneous data stream types: commodity futures, shipping equities, freight rate proxies, foreign exchange stress indicators, logistics equities, geopolitical event feeds (GDELT), and public attention signals (Wikipedia pageviews). The Supply Chain Stress Index (SCSI), a composite scoring metric at the core of the system, unifies per-stream Isolation Forest anomaly scores through weighted aggregation, exponential moving average smoothing, and a four-tier calibrated alert hierarchy. Retrospective replay-mode evaluation across four historically significant events-the 2021 Suez Canal blockage, the 2022 Russia-Ukraine supply shock, the 2023 Red Sea maritime security crisis, and COVID-19 port bottlenecks (2020-21)-demonstrates HIGH-tier detection at zero-day latency for two acute events (peak SCSI 0.611 and 0.592 respectively), ELEVATED-tier detection within one day for a sustained maritime security crisis, and correct Normal classification during gradual logistical stress accumulation. False positive rates at the HIGH threshold are 0.00 across all pre-event baseline windows. Taken together, these results demonstrate that purpose-built IoT streaming architectures can materially advance the temporal frontier of operational supply chain situational awareness.

title: Playing it Safe? The Effect of Abortion Bans on Sexual Behavior
affiliations: Miami University of Ohio - Richard T. Farmer School of Business Administration, Middlebury College and Middlebury College

detail.title: Playing it Safe? The Effect of Abortion Bans on Sexual Behavior
detail.abstract:
We estimate the effect of total abortion bans enacted after Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health on sexual behavior. Using synthetic and standard difference-in-differences designs, we analyze gonorrhea rates and over-the-counter contraceptive purchases as indicators of sexual activity and contraceptive use. We find that total abortion bans reduced gonorrhea rates by 21% among the population aged 15–44 and increased condom purchases by 5.4%. County-level analyses suggest the response reflects awareness of state policy rather than changes in travel distance to providers. These findings are consistent with a framework in which abortion restrictions increase the perceived cost of unprotected sex, inducing more cautious behavior.

title: Spectral PELVE and Cross-Border Tail-Shape Connectedness in Global Equity Markets
affiliations: Izmir Bakircay University/Department of Economics and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Spectral PELVE and Cross-Border Tail-Shape Connectedness in Global Equity Markets
detail.abstract: We propose a spectral framework for monitoring the cross-border transmission of tail-shape risk among international equity markets, oriented toward financial-stability surveillance. The framework combines the Probability Equivalent Level of Value-at-Risk and Expected Shortfall (PELVE), a location- and scale-invariant index of tail shape motivated by the Basel III FRTB shift from VaR to ES, with wavelet multiresolution analysis and a time-varying parameter vector autoregression (TVP-VAR). Applying the framework to fifteen markets partitioned into G7, structurally intermediate, and BRICS blocks over 2012-2026, we document four findings of relevance to systemic-risk monitoring. First, block-average PELVE lies above the Gaussian tail-shape benchmark at the 5% tail level and above the FRTB-motivated probability-multiplier reference, rising markedly once the COVID-19 shock enters the rolling estimation window. This pattern is pervasive across blocks and horizons, consistent with the prudential rationale for the VaR-to-ES transition. Second, the G7 block is the largest net transmitter of tail-shape spillovers at every investment horizon, while the structurally intermediate and BRICS blocks absorb comparable spillovers at short and medium horizons but diverge at the longer-horizon component, where the intermediate block absorbs more. Third, the two reported crisis regimes are associated with opposing connectedness patterns: the COVID-19 window is associated with a total connectedness index up to 20 percentage points above tranquil levels, consistent with broad-based synchronization, whereas the Russia--Ukraine window is associated with lower connectedness and a smaller BRICS contribution to cross-block spillovers, consistent with fragmentation. Fourth, comparing the G7-BRICS core with the full system shows that the structurally intermediate block adds 13.8 to 16.4 percentage points of measured system connectedness, so that surveillance frameworks omitting such markets may understate global tail-shape connectedness. The framework provides a market-based, frequency-resolved diagnostic indicator that can support financial-stability surveillance of cross-border tail-shape risk.

title: From Trade War to Green Transition: Optimal Electric Vehicle Tariffs with Revenue-Funded Subsidies
affiliations: Cornell University - Department of Economics, University of Wisconsin-Madison - Department of Economics, Yale University - Department of Economics, Stanford University and

detail.title: From Trade War to Green Transition: Optimal Electric Vehicle Tariffs with Revenue-Funded Subsidies
detail.abstract:
We study the optimal design of trade and industrial policy when governments pursue environmental objectives alongside traditional welfare goals. Motivated by the global transition to electric vehicles (EVs) and growing concerns about competitiveness, energy security, and climate change, we develop a framework in which policymakers choose tariffs and domestic production subsidies to maximize welfare, defined as the sum of consumer surplus, domestic profits, environmental benefits, and tariff revenue. We combine a theoretical model of differentiated-product oligopoly with a structural demand model estimated using vehicle-level data from 13 countries that together account for the vast majority of global EV sales. Our central finding is that the optimal policy combines a moderate tariff on imported EVs with a subsidy to domestic EV production financed through tariff revenue. This policy substantially outperforms both outright protectionism and laissez-faire. Relative to current policies, it preserves consumer access to affordable EVs, accelerates fleet electrification, supports domestic producers, and remains budget-neutral. For the United States, the optimal policy more than doubles EV market share, generates over $45 billion in annual welfare gains, and avoids approximately 95 million tons of lifetime CO2 emissions. A key mechanism underlying these results is the pass-through of tariffs and subsidies to prices, which depends critically on demand curvature, product substitution, and market structure. More broadly, our results suggest that effective industrial policy requires careful attention to market structure and country-specific conditions, balancing consumer, producer, fiscal, and environmental objectives rather than adhering to ideological prescriptions.

title: A Comprehensive Global Assessment of Financial Mechanisms for Green Financial Recovery and Climate Change Mitigation: Insights from the Case Study of China
affiliations: Fudan University

detail.title: A Comprehensive Global Assessment of Financial Mechanisms for Green Financial Recovery and Climate Change Mitigation: Insights from the Case Study of China
detail.abstract: As nations increasingly resume life and industrial production post-pandemic, the effects of climate change have exacerbated health crises globally, highlighting the urgent need for green economic recovery measures. This article explores the environmental and economic implications of climate change across different regions of China, both in the present and looking ahead. Utilizing a popular computable general equilibrium (CGE) method, this study examines the post-pandemic effects of various fiscal strategies—including revenue losses and increased spending—alongside the implementation of a carbon tax.The global economic shocks experienced from March 21, 2020, to July 3, 2021, have significantly disadvantaged regional economies worldwide. Our empirical findings reveal that the economic impacts of the COVID-19 pandemic have been sustained and are likely to further inhibit economic activity.Notably, among the government's recovery strategies, reductions in indirect taxes have proven most beneficial to regional economies, particularly in areas targeted for zero carbon emissions. Additionally, strategies aimed at minimizing the damage from green economic recovery could benefit from substituting indirect production taxes with carbon taxes. We develop long-term indicators to measure performance against standard global economic metrics, and our empirical results indicate a significant correlation with economic recovery indicators, offering important policy implications.
